utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, may I ask you to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around are the courtroom. This is case number IT-00-39-A, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. May I ask Mr. Krajisnik if he can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I can follow in my language, and I can hear well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Let me now call for appearances. For Mr. Krajisnik's counsel on the matter of JCE, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Nathan Dershowitz, JCE counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Peter Kremer, Mr. President and members of the Court, appearing for the Prosecution. Assisting me this morning are Mr. Matteo Costi and Ms. Katharina Margetts and our case manager, Alma Imamovic-Ivanov is also assisting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now for the amicus curiae.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colin Nicholls acting as -- sorry. Colin Nicholls acting as amicus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is an evidentiary hearing on appeal in the case of the Prosecutor against Krajisnik. Today we will hear the testimony of Mr. George Mano and Mr. Stefan Karganovic who were summoned by the Appeal Chamber on October 2008 under Rules 98 and 107 of the Rules. Let me briefly summarise the evidence, which have ben admitted in this appeal and it will detail the order in which we hear the witnesses' testimonies today. First, in its decision of 20 August 2008, the Appeals Chamber admitted into evidence under Rule 115 statements by Mr. Mano and Mr. Karganovic, both presented by the Defence. Mr. Mano's statement is Exhibit AD1 and that of Mr. Karganovic is Exhibit AD2. In its decision of 8 October 2008, the Appeals Chamber admitted seven document presented by the Prosecution as rebuttal evidence to these statements its exhibits AP1 to AP7. I would like to remind the parties that Exhibits AD1 and AD2 as well as the rebuttal evidence are under seal. Therefore if the parties or amicus curiae wish to refer to these documents they should request private session. This morning we will first hear Witness George Mano. He appears as a witness of the Appeals Chamber. The main examination will therefore be conducted by the Bench. Mr. Krajisnik will then have the opportunity of questioning Mr. Mano for 45 minutes, after which the Prosecution and amicus curiae may pose questions to the witness for 45 minutes each. We will then break and after lunch the Bench will examine Witness Karganovic who is also a Chamber witness, and we will follow the same -- the same schedule as for the testimony of Mr. Mano. We will rise, of course, for the usual breaks every one and a half hours during the morning and the afternoon, and as usual the time allotted to the parties is approximate and may with leave of the Chamber be varied where necessary. That said, I wish to remind the parties that they are not oblige to use ought time allocated, and as always, Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions to the witnesses. So having said that about the manner in which we will proceed today, I would now like to call Witness George Mano.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address the Chamber for one second with respect to the schedule?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: I had assumed on the basis of the orders of the Court and the time schedule now that the amicus would be inquiring of the witnesses on ineffective assistance of counsel and therefore would include within their area of inquiry questions relating to JCE. I was advised last night and again this morning that amicus is probably not going to cover that area because of a lack of clarity as to whether that is within the ambit of their area of responsibility. So under those circumstances, if they choose not to inquire into the JCE area, I with like with the permission of Mr. Nicholls to be able to take ten minutes of the allocated time that they have to make some inquiries, if it's not covered by the Chamber before, with respect to ineffective assistance of counsel solely as it relates to the JCE issue. And of course if necessary I can request from Mr. Krajisnik that I take ten of his minutes instead of Mr. Nicholls' ten minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I consulted my colleagues and this could be appropriate. You certainly can do that taking from the time either of the -- of Mr. Krajisnik also or of the amicus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I make my position clear as amicus? I do not intend to cross-examine either of the witnesses for reasons which I've already placed before the Chamber, and there is one additional reason in the case of the witness Mr. Karganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I take note of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now, good morning, Mr. Mano.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Could you please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mano. You may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I refer to notes if I'm not sure about a date or a fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Of course you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court your full name and date of birth first?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: George Mano, July 24, 1961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your address? *A. The street address or city?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay. I live at 202 Honmachi in Himeji Japan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us what education you have and give us a brief list of your previous and present occupation.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I teach English at a university in Japan. I've been living in Japan for 13 years. For the past ten years, I've been teaching at the university where I am currently employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mano, the Court has asked you to testify in the appeals proceeding in the case of the Prosecutor against Momcilo Krajisnik. As it is the Court itself that has requested your attendance, you will first be asked questions by the Judges. As I am the Presiding Judge, I will begin the questioning myself, following questions by the other Judges. You may then be asked questions by Mr. Krajisnik, the Prosecution, and the amicus curiae. Specifically, we will be asking you questions as to what you know about the workings of Mr. Krajisnik's Defence team during trial and the conduct of former counsel Nicholas Stewart in relation thereto. Now, first, Mr. Mano, did you work for Mr. Krajisnik's Defence team during his trial?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes. I was a volunteer intern in the summer of 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: How long did you work in the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Approximately three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And that is from, to?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I started on July 5th, and my last day was September 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Apart from this, have you had or do you have any other working relationship with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I guess last year or maybe earlier this year Mr. Krajisnik, when he took over his own defence, named me as one of his team for his appeal; but I was not paid a salary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: What were your duties within the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Are you referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: During the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, I had various duties. I read documents that had been given to the Defence from the Prosecution relating to facts that the Prosecution and the Defence were asked to agree upon. I prepared cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. I wrote historical background of the war for the Defence, and I also prepared a list or a packet of information about expert witnesses for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Why did you leave the Defence team? Sorry. I didn't have the microphone. Why did you leave the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, I had a full-time job in Japan. I only agreed to work for three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the work -- your work with the Defence team, what was your professional relation to Defence counsel, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, I was a volunteer, an intern, an unpaid clerk, if you will, for the Defence team. So he was my boss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And for how long did you interact with Mr. Stewart in this capacity?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: For the entire time I was here. From July 5th until September 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now, moving to another question. Have you worked or are you currently working on other cases before this Tribunal or any other international criminal tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I assisted one other case briefly when I was here in the summer of 2004. And when I say briefly, one day. I was asked by another Defence team if I would help them review their final brief for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us which was the case?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I don't remember the name of the case, but the lead attorney was Michael Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I will now move to asking you something about the exhibit unless there are other questions that my colleagues want to put before I do that. We have to go into private session. Thank you. Because the exhibit is under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So first since we are dealing with Exhibit AD1, can the witness be presented with the exhibit. So, Mr. Mano, this document is a letter of -- dated September 23, 2004, addressed by you to Mr. Van de Vliet of the Tribunal's office of legal aid and detention. Could you please take a moment to familiarise yourself with the document. Can you confirm that you wrote this letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes. This looks like the letter I wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Does the letter represent the truth to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, I would like to turn your attention specifically to page 3 of the letter stating that there is convincing evidence that Mr. Stewart should not be left to handle this case. Am I correct to understand from your letter that you reach this conclusion based on Mr. Stewart's statement before the Trial Chamber that he did not know whether or not Mr. Krajisnik was innocent?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. Probably I should have said that this statement, along with everything else, should be convincing to anyone that he should not be left to handle this case. But I did feel at the time that that statement was completely out of line and would not be the statement made by a competent attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, could you explain the circumstances under which Mr. Stewart made this statement?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay. I believe I -- okay. I did write that this was made during an oral argument. I'm not really sure if it was during an oral argument. It may have been during cross-examination of a witness. I can't recall at the time, but he was talking to the Court, and I don't remember the exact circumstances, but this statement by Mr. Stewart came out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Let me take another point of the letter. At the bottom of page 1, continuing on page 2 of your letter, you claim that Mr. Stewart wanted to agree with the Prosecution to facts which in your view are detrimental to Mr. Krajisnik's Defence. You give one example concerning what you call a Serbian gang leader. Were there are other examples of Mr. Stewart agreeing to facts that detrimental to Mr. Krajisnik's Defence.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. Probably I should give you a little more information about that. It was the second day I was here at the Tribunal when I was given a list of these statements of facts to review before Mr. Stewart and one or two other members of the team met with the Prosecution team to discuss these facts and to agree upon some of them or all of them; and we went to that meeting that day - I believe it was in the afternoon - and it was clear to me that Mr. Stewart was agreeing to a lot of things that could not be confirm or should not be confirmed that were highly detrimental to Mr. Krajisnik's defence. So the next morning I sent an e-mail to Mr. Stewart to meet with him because I wanted to tell him I was a little bit concerned about this and maybe he should spend a little more time or be a little bit more careful about the facts that he was agreeing to. So I met with him. I believe it was late that morning on the -- that would have been the 8th of July, and he basically told me that I didn't understand how the court worked and that it didn't matter what facts he agreed to because it wouldn't harm the case. And that didn't seem a very convincing argument to me, but I was no position to do or say anything about it; but I thought he will certainly never invite me again to one of these meetings. However, later that day they had another meeting, and apparently he didn't feel that the Defence team had enough members, so he grabbed me from the Defence room and said could I join them. So we went into the meeting with the Prosecutors, and I believe there were three at that meeting. That would have been Mr. Harmon, Mr. Tieger, and Mr. Gaynor, and there was one fact in there that really bothered me. It said that this man, this Serbian gang member -- or gang leader, excuse me, was a member of the SDS. So I asked Mr. Harmon how did you know he was a member of the SDS. Did you discover his SDS party membership card? Did he announce publicly that he was a member of the SDS, and Mr. Harmon said, No but he worked hand in glove with members of the SDS. And I said, Well that isn't what it says here it says he's a member of the SDS. And Mr. Harmon said, Okay I'll remove it and Mr. Stewart said, No, no. Let's leave it in. This was after Mr. Harmon say he would remove him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. May I turn to another point. On page 1 you state that Mr. Stewart admitted in court that at the time he took on the position of lead counsel he only had "an intelligent person's knowledge of the facts of the case."

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. I think he said an educated, layman's knowledge, isn't that what the said? Or I'm sorry I misquoted it here. I think what he said is, "I had an average educated layman's knowledge," something like that. You can find that statement in his oral argument on July 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. You then say that Mr. Stewart subsequently, that again I'm quoting your letter "added very little to that storehouse of knowledge." Apart from the examples mentioned in your letter, do you have any other examples supporting this assertion?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, it was -- besides those particular facts because there were many other of these factual agreements between the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Besides on these particular facts.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: You want a specific example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: On the knowledge you have more facts supporting an assertion that he add very little to that storehouse of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay. Off the top of my head I don't think I can give you a specific example, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. On page 2 of your letter, I'm turning to another issue, I think it's the last paragraph, yes, you say that Mr. Stewart treated Mr. Krajisnik as his enemy. On what basis did you reach such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Some of his comments to me privately. He -- as I said, he made that statement to me when we were riding in the car one day, that he said that in England they -- barristers say that the client is the enemy, and there were many occasions -- or I shouldn't say many. There were several occasions where he said to me -- or where he complained about Mr. Krajisnik privately. That was the basis of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: On page 2 of your letter you state again that Mr. Stewart took, and I quote "little personal interest in the outcome of the case." And you exemplify this by stating that he spent time abroad for personal reasons instead of preparing for the case. Can you elaborate on this?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. I found it very ironic that on July 14th he filed a motion for adjournment, and then there was oral argument on July 16th for adjournment. He was asking for three months to prepare for the case, and then soon after the judgement came in that his motion was denied he went on a vacation to Croatia for nine days, and he frequently was -- was gone, you know, for one- or two-day periods during the time that I was there. He also made a trip to Spain in September, from September 18th he was gone for ten days. If he really was so short on time why was he taking these personal vacations. And then everything else was handled in kind of haphazard disorganised way. It didn't seem like there was a lot of thought going into how he could best serve this defendant, and I -- I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, can you tell us if you ever raised the issues you are raising in your letter directly with Mr. Stewart or with the Trial Chamber before sending the letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It was very tough to talk to Mr. Stewart. As I mentioned in my letter, he had a very condescending tone with people that he thought were inferior to him. To raise this kind of issue with him would have been very difficult. There may have been one or two times where I gave suggestions where I thought his defence was going in the wrong direction, and he immediately dismissed them. And as I mentioned in my letter, that everyone working around him after a while just gave up trying to give him advice because he wouldn't accept any outside advice from anyone. Unless he came up with the idea on his own, he wasn't going to implement it. And I should also meant that I believe Chrissa Loukas was having some problems, and I know that she asked to be removed from the case shortly after I left. So I think she had some problems also. Problems with Mr. Stewart, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You believe that or -- or did Ms. Loukas confide to you what she thought of Mr. Stewart in the case?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: She expressed frustration on at least one or two occasions, and there was one incident that I probably wasn't supposed to be privy to. I went into -- came into the Tribunal on the weekend to use the internet to check my e-mail because I didn't have internet access in my apartment, and in the fax machine was a letter, a private letter to Ms. Loukas that said that she was asking the -- some legal body in Australia for -- to be promoted as lead counsel for the Krajisnik case. I believe that was the content of it, but you'd have to ask her about that. I think I'm the only person outside of Ms. Loukas who knows about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you want to state anything else regarding the issues raised in the letter? Which I have not raised, I mean, with you today.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Just that I should also mention -- it wasn't mentioned in this letter, but it was mentioned in a later letter to Mr. Van de Vliet that the Defence was really disorganised. There seemed to be no plan as to how the Defence was going to proceed. Everything was a brush fire that had to be put out immediately. So I -- that was another one of my concerns was the disorganisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron, you want to put a question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, you mentioned several absences from the trial --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. Mr. Mano, you mentioned several absences of Mr. Stewart from the trial. During those periods what was happening? Did Ms. Loukas proceed with the trial? Was the trial suspended or ...

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: In the month of August, for example, there were no courtroom debts -- courtroom dates set, so it was time that we could use for research. When Nicholas Stewart left most of us just continue doing the research we were doing before he left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So the trial was not continuing during his absences.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: There were no trial dates during those absences; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, may I ask you whether you ever discussed the contents of your letter with Mr. Karganovic or any other member of the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: This letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes, I have discussed it with Mr. Karganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: When, before sending the letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, no. Not before sending it. He was not a member of the team at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: When did you discuss it with Mr. Karganovic?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It might have been a year or so later. I am not sure when he took over the job of case manager for Mr. Krajisnik, but it was sometime after that. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Karganovic wrote a statement on 16 October 2007 containing certain allegations against Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I didn't know the date. I know that he was -- that he had in mind the intent to write a letter. I have never seen the letter. I don't know the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And you said he discussed with Mr. Karganovic the content of your letter. When you discussed that was before 16 October 2007 or after that date.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It was probably before, and I believe he told me at the time that he had seen my letter in a file when he took over the job as case manager; but again I'm not sure about that. You'd have to ask him that question. The first time I talked to him about it was much later anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: What do you mean much later?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Much later than I sent it to Mr. Van de Vliet and before the date you mentioned October 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So before the date.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Right sometime in between those two dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So you discussed before Mr. Karganovic sent his letter on 16 October 2007.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I have no other questions at the moment unless my colleagues have questions. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, when you discussed the contents of your letter with Mr. Karganovic, did he at that time have any professional connection with the case?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. He was the case manager at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. Mano.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to go back in time a bit. Could you please be more specific in relation to something that has to do with Ms. Loukas. You said that one day you came to the Tribunal at -- and that you saw a letter for Ms. Loukas where she was asking to be promoted to the lead counsel not Krajisnik case. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I said a fax, yeah. It was a fax letter. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how come you were able to see this fax?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It was sitting in the fax machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. And you didn't speak to Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: About the letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes the examination from the Bench. I will now turn to Mr. Krajisnik. If he wants to question Mr. Mano, he is allowed to do that. Please, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mano.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In your letter, which was sent to the representative of OLAD, you present a number of criticism in relation to the work of my attorney. I will present them briefly even though His Honour Judge Pocar has already mentioned them in a way. You said that Mr. Stewart was not familiar with the historical -- historic background the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question to you is what is your speciality? What is your occupation, actually?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I teach at a university in Japan. My main job is to teach English to Japanese students at the university. However, the first four years I was there I also taught a course on modern Eastern Europe. I have a Masters Degree in history, specialising in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That means, if I can put it that way, that you are -- that you have an educational background in history and you are familiar with the events in the Balkans between 1980 and 1995 -- 1990 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I'm somewhat familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. In your letter you said that Mr. Stewart did not want to accept any advice relating to his insufficiently of his knowledge of the historic background in Balkans. Did you try to suggest to him that you were somebody who knew more about those issues than he did?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I never said any such thing, but I did correct him on occasion, and as I said, it wasn't only about the historical background of the Balkans that Mr. Stewart did not want to hear about. It was any subject. He would not take advice or criticism from anyone that he deemed was inferior to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In your letter, as far as I could understand, you say that he had a condescending attitude towards his associates who would try to give him advice. Is that the feeling you had also whether it came to his attitude toward you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You also said that he really wasn't very interested in the Krajisnik case. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this: You said here that you know that he had frequent or almost daily contact with the Prosecution. Did he also have contact with the Trial Chamber or officers of the Trial Chamber? Do you know whether he had meetings with them or had written communication with them?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't know if I said he had frequent or almost daily contact with the Prosecution. Concerning the statements of facts, he did meet with them for several days, and I was aware that he was receiving e-mail from the Prosecution during that time period. As far as the Trial Chamber goes, I -- I couldn't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you know whether he wrote to the Trial Chamber in relation to any problem he may have encountered during his defence work?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: You mean outside of the normal legal documents relating to motions and objections and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, let me be specific. Did he write to the Trial Chamber in order to warn them or to express concern about not having proper conditions for work and that he needed adjournment for those reasons?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, he filed a motion for adjournment on July 14th, and he argued orally on July 16th for an adjournment. In that oral argument, he made a number of statements which everyone, of course, can read. It's a matter of public record. That he needed more time, that his staff was overworked, and he was overworked and so on. As I said, it's a matter of public record. Everyone can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: All right. With the permission of the Appeals Chamber and everybody else, I would like to ask you to take a look at the documents which have been prepared for you. I would like to compare some of these parts of the documents with your statement. Therefore, would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I was handed a package of documents this morning. I'm not sure if the Chamber has. Perhaps it not be handed out yet. I gather from the preliminary remarks Mr. Krajisnik has just made relating to the question that he is about to introduce through Mr. -- or attempt to introduce through Mr. Mano documents of which he knows nothing. His testimony already confirms that. And as far as I know, the documents all are subsequent to Mr. Mano's employment with the Tribunal and employment with the Defence team. So I'm just putting the Chamber on notice. The Chamber has these documents by way of a supplementary 115 application by Mr. Krajisnik and has not yet ruled on them, and it relates to the testimony potentially of Mr. Stewart and Ms. Loukas and Alexander Zahar. I would object to any questions relating to these documents because the witness has no knowledge of them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I just intervene as amicus for a moment? These --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Micro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't press it clearly enough. These documents obviously are of considerable importance. The question is of course in what way can they be introduced into evidence. The only issue that does occur to me that may be of relevance is that the documents themselves may contain matters of historic value on which the witness may be able to express a view or which the witness may be able to confirm. I merely say that because at some stage the Chamber may wish to consider whether these documents should be introduce into evidence and in particular who should introduce them.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I also address that question for one moment? It would appear to me that if Mr. Stewart's own writings confirm the testimony of the witness, the witness should be able to review those documents and say, The writings of Mr. Stewart, the attitude reflected in those documents, the statements that he made are all consistent with my prior observations as reflected in my letter; and that of course would be extremely important to the Tribunal. If the Tribunal sees that a witness in 2004 indicated concerns with Mr. Stewart's attitude toward the case and subsequent documents written by Mr. Stewart confirm that, whether this witness is the appropriate person or not, it is clearly of extreme value to the Tribunal in deciding the question of ineffective assistance of counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If I could -- Mr. President, with your permission. I don't disagree with what my colleagues opposite have just said. The statements to the extent that they're relevant to the time-frame that this witness was with the Tribunal can certainly be put. My objection is in relation to tendering these documents as exhibits and for Your Honours giving them full weight without the proper person who prepared the document being present to introduce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, on some of these documents there is a motion pending on admissibility on which the Chamber has not pronounced yet. I believe these documents should not be brought today into evidence, and -- but of course nothing prevents Mr. Krajisnik of putting questions to the witness without, without, documents being shown to the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much, Your Honours. I would now need to reduce the amount of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Let me ask you had this, Mr. Mano: When you came to Mr. Stewart, did you know Krajisnik at that time?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by the question. Did I know who you were, or did I know you personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Did you know me personally? Had you met me by that time?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I've never met you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with me during the trial while you were a member of Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, I asked Nicholas Stewart if I could go to meet you during one of his regular meetings with you in the penitentiary, and I always -- he always came up with some excuse why I couldn't go. I thought about going alone, but I was told I could not go without permission of the lead counsel. So I have never met you until today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Does that mean that before sending this letter you had no contacts with me in order to consult me about the letter or in order to receive a consent from me for sending the letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct. My goal in sending the letter, as I stated, was to inform you, Mr. Krajisnik, about a situation that I thought you might not be aware of but that you needed to know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, if I understood this correctly, these exhibits will not be -- these documents will not be admitted into evidence; but it was my understanding that I could refer to certain quotations so that Mr. Mano can confirm whether what is in these documents corresponds with his statement. May I ask for clarification from the Chamber? Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you can put -- state facts or statements to the witness and ask the witness if they correspond to his -- to his knowledge or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you, because you have some documents in front of you, to find among these documents Exhibit number 3. Since I do not speak the English language, I would like to ask Mr. Mano to help me and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you can't refer to the documents as such. The witness does not have the documents. So you may only refer to statements or dispose facts and ask the witness to confirm or not confirm what you are saying, but you are not allowed to refer to specific documents. You can't ask the witness to -- to look at an exhibit, because the witness does not have the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: There is an indication that the Trial Chamber at the time thought that Mr. Stewart was arrogant, unpleasant, and that in a way acted to the detriment of Krajisnik's defence. Does this correspond to the observation you made in your statement?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I don't know if it corresponds to my statement, but I would certainly agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Also, there is an indication that the Trial Chamber at a meeting -- or, rather, a representative of the Trial Chamber objected to Mr. Stewart to the effect that he uses adjournments in the trial to take care of his private problems, as it were, and also to deal with some cases in London. Is this indication in a way identical to what it was that you observed when you were with Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: He certainly had some private problems that he would sometimes take time off for. As far -- and he did go to London. At least I know of one situation on July 21st. He went to London which -- and I believe that was for taking care of business there. So certainly that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If I put it to you that it is indicated in a particular document that the Trial Chamber is of the position that Mr. Stewart is not using his time for preparation but that, rather, in fact he is shifting the burden to the shoulders of his co-counsel, which is one the reasons why this co-counsel left the trial and the Defence team. Is that your impression? Is that the impression you gain at the time when you were involved in the trial and in contact with Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't know exactly Chrissa Loukas wanted to leave. She never told me her exact reasons. But it wouldn't surprise me if that was one of the reasons why she left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Let me ask you something. If I put it to you hypothetically that in the contacts between Mr. Stewart and the representatives of the Trial Chamber he received an answer that he noted down in his own notes that the Trial Chamber, but not only the Trial Chamber but also the Registry was unsatisfied with his work because they said that he was not a successful manager and that he didn't know how to organise the work of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I would -- I would believe that completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: At the time when you were on the Defence team, did you see that Mr. Stewart had a plan as how to conduct the Krajisnik defence?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I saw no such plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: But can you give your own judgement on the basis of the experience you have that Mr. Stewart, as he was taking certain steps like the example that you refer to, accepting facts that were not facts, that that was a strategic decision or a different kind of decision? If it's a different kind of decision, could you please explain what would be the consequence of that kind of decision of his?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I thought his defence was chaotic. I don't think he had a well thought out plan. As I said earlier he seemed to rush from one brush fire to another. There were one or two occasions where we would get an e-mail and he'd say -- or sometimes an e-mail, sometimes a phone call where he would say, "I need research on this topic right away. I have to do something tomorrow on it." That didn't sound like he had thought about this until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In your letter you say that he did have respect for -- I beg your pardon for this comparison, that he had respect for big fish but not for small fry. He considered some members of the Prosecution team not to be his equals. Does that show what Mr. Stewart's attitude was vis-a-vis the other side?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes. I gave an example of that in my letter. I certainly thought Mr. Harmon and Mr. Tieger were his equals, but he didn't think that about Mr. Gaynor and probably some of the other people on the Prosecution team. And I gave the example of one occasion where Mr. Gaynor took over the Prosecution's case that day, and Mr. Stewart left this room that we're in -- well, it might not have been this room but one of these rooms and left the trial to Ms. Loukas that day; and he said to me outside that he wasn't going to stay there because there were only minnows was the word he used. I believe that he said that there were only minnows in the room, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You said that you worked on preparing witness statements. How did you carry out this work? If my understanding of your work is correct, what is exactly the kind of work you did for Mr. Stewart in this respect?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: The witnesses were deposed before they were brought to court to testify, and we were given copies of their depositions, and if it was my duty for that particular witness to examine the deposition and look for contradictions or statements that were obviously false, I would read -- well, I would read through the deposition and make little notes, and then I would type up my type findings and hand those to Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You are talking about Prosecution witnesses, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct. At the time the Prosecution was presenting its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As for experts, you referred to experts, in contact with Mr. Stewart did you get any response as to whether he would call any expert witnesses? If so, who and how many experts, and also for what facts he wanted to call expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, one of my -- one of the other members of the team, Brett Taxin made a list of expert witnesses from other cases that had already taken place in the Tribunal; and I was preparing a document that included some of those witnesses but additional witnesses that I thought we might call. I prepared a booklet that included the names of these potential witnesses and the content of their potential testimony as well as copies of any publications I could find on the internet, and I handed this entire package to Chrissa Loukas, as far as I know. Well, as far as I know. I don't know if Mr. Stewart even looked at it. I don't know what he did with it. The only thing I receive from him regarding expert witnesses what is an e-mail. I can look up the date. If I can take a moment to find it I can tell you what date that was. Would that be all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Just while the witness is looking at the documents, in the jurisdiction where I practised law if the witness comes to court with the documents that the parties haven't seen the parties are entitled to see those documents, and if I ask during the break if the witness would allow me to review his notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: If I may. In the jurisdiction where I practice, it is a question as to whether the witness uses the information, not whether he --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Dershowitz.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. I think the document he looks at to refresh his recollection should be made available, but I don't think the other materials that he happens to carry into court should be turned over simply for that reason, that he carried it into court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Of course we agree. We are referring to the documents that he makes use of, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm saying only the ones he makes use of. Mr. Kremer says anything he brought into court. That's the distinction, I think, we're making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I would believe that the documents that are actually used and consulted should be -- should be disclosed to the parties, but other documents, of course, that remain in the -- in the briefcase or suitcase of the witness remain there and -- and will not have to be disclose. Well, could you refresh your memory on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes I received an e-mail message on Sunday, July 18th, in reference to expert testimony because I had asked to take the day -- or to not come to the Tribunal the following day, which was Monday, because I wanted to go to the library at this University of Leiden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik, you can continue with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You prepared some documentation on the basis of which Mr. Stewart was supposed to decide which experts to call. My question is the following: In your assessment, was it hard for Mr. Stewart to select experts and to call them? Was there a technical problem involved?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Actually, I can't answer that question, but I can tell you what he said in this e-mail if that's permissible. Should I read what he said about expert testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. He said: "We have to approach it as follows: One, prioritise our needs for experts in particular areas. Two, identify suitable experts in the priority areas. And three, prepare a rigorous and compelling case for funding from the Registry."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your answer is just fine. Now I would like to put a few more questions only. Did Mr. Stewart tell you that he had a plan as to exactly what type of expert he would like to call?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Next question: Did you ever talk to Mr. Stewart and caution him to the effect that it was very important for him to be aware of the historical background of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I mentioned that at least on at least one occasion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In your view was he prepared or, rather, did he have a satisfactory knowledge of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially the war that is the subject of this trial?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, he did not, and that's one of the reasons I spent several weeks putting together a document which was a short summary of the background information, the historical background for the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, your actual line of work is that of an historian.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's one of my lines of work, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In your view, although perhaps this is not a proper question, are you qualified to give suggestions to him in or to help him learn about what he didn't know concerning the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I don't have a document which says that I'm an expert, by think that I have sufficient knowledge to inform someone about the background of the conflict, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And may I state, if I understood you correctly, that Mr. Stewart did not accept your proposals or the proposals of other associates when these questions were being discussed?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: When any question was being discussed. He didn't like to have advice from subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Specifically in terms of historical context, could you just give an answer to that question? As far as the historical background is concerned, he was not prepared to take any advice from anyone?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As far as I can see on the basis of your CV, you are a lawyer as well.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I have a JD, but I'm not a member of the bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: But you have a degree in law; right? That is your education?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself to be qualified to assess the quality of the work of a lawyer in proceedings such as mine?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It would depend, but in this case I think you would not need to have a JD to see that Mr. Stewart was not managing the defence very effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would like to go back to this question nevertheless. As a person who has a degree in law, you could assess the strategy of the defence. Do you think that you were meritorious in terms of assessing the strategy that he had or didn't have? If he did have one it was a poor one, as you said. And then there is this other statement that indicates that there was some strain and -- well, could you as a lawyer assess that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I would -- my assessment would be based on my short experience working for a law firm in the United States, and the way that law firm was run was a lot different than the way Mr. Stewart was running the defence for -- for you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Does this now correspond to a particular indication that we have in some documents that we are not going to tender today but that we did provide to the Appeals Chamber in which we see that the representative of the Trial Chamber concludes that Mr. Stewart was not a good organiser, was not a good manager of the case?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: He was disorganised, and he wasted time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: All right. Now let me ask you whether Mr. Stewart ever raised a question pertaining to joint criminal enterprise with the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: One of the -- one of my colleagues, I believe it was Thomas Derrington, I'd have to check my notes, prepared a document about it at my suggestion, because when I arrived I asked if there was a memo stating the general background of the laws that were relevant to this case; and he said there was no such memo, and then he began to prepare one. Besides that document, I didn't see anything about joint criminal enterprise; and I don't think I ever heard it mention by Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Mano, I would just like to put a question to you. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber in a bit more detail what your motive was to write a letter concerning a man you did not know, to write about irregular conduct of a man who worked with you or, rather, who you volunteered to work with? And what was the reason for you to insist with the Registry to have that letter presented to me as well, because at first the Registry did not send that letter to me and did not make me aware of it; you did not send that letter to me. You sent it to the Registry, and it was supposed to reach me through the Registry. I would just like you to describe this for me. What was your reason? Was it a personal reason perhaps? Did it have to do with the credibility of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, that's a number of questions. I'll try to answer all of them. First of all, I have no personal grudge against Mr. Stewart, and that was not a motivation. I have no strong feelings about him in any kind of way. My motivation was to merely right what I thought was a terrible injustice going on. I realised that although some of my colleagues had expressed their doubts about the quality of defence to me privately, that no one was going to do anything about it publicly. This was partly due to the fact that a lot of them depended on letters of recommendation from Mr. Stewart for their future careers. Since I do not work in law and I basically have a secure job at a university, I didn't need a letter of recommendation from Mr. Stewart. I thought I was in a position to do something, and that if I didn't do something about it, if I didn't at least make the Registry and the Tribunal aware of what was going on; and you specifically, if I didn't let you know specifically what was going on with your defence, that I would be allowing a terrible injustice to continue. It's kind of like if you know a building is going to burn down you should do something about it. You should call the fire department. You should not just let it burn. And that's how I felt. So I -- before I left, I contacted Mr. Van de Vliet, made an appointment with him, and I typed up the letter that you see and I handed it to him because I wasn't sure how long I would have to talk to him. I thought I better put something down on paper to get it on the record. And in my discussion I said, "My main goal in giving this to you is for you to have it translated and put in the hands of Mr. Krajisnik," and he gave me his assurance that that would happen. He say, "I give you my word." And as we know he broke his word, because he didn't put it in your hands. The first thing he did was hand it over to Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart, I don't know what he told him because I've never seen Mr. Stewart's reply, and I -- I don't know if I can ask the Tribunal to provide that to me, but I would -- I'd be interested to see what his reply was. But in any case, he did not translate it and hand it to you. He said he was not going to do that. So I had to find another means of getting that letter into your hands, and I asked the translator from another case to translate it for me and to fax it to you, and that's how it finally got into your hands several weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, it's 10.00. Judge Guney, you have a question to put, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for you, Mr. Mano, a question of general nature. You have said that you worked with the former counsel Mr. Stewart for three months and that you did so without pay. You were a volunteer. Given the practical difficulties that you came across during those three months, what was your main reason for accepting to work as a volunteer, and what was your main reason for continuing with this work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a good question, because I think everyone who works here has different motivations. Some people are probably doing it to advance their careers. Some people are probably doing it for the money. In my case, it was neither one of those because my career is entirely unrelated to my work in the Tribunal, and I wasn't paid for it. Obviously from my background in history and from my background in law, I saw this as an opportunity to work in both of those areas and still keep my job in Japan. I realised I couldn't give up my job in Japan and come here permanently, and I don't know if I could even work here permanently; but I saw the option of coming here for the summer as an intern as a wonderful chance not only to improve my knowledge of the events in the Balkans and also get a little bit of law experience in as well, but also to use my background in law and history to hopefully do something good. So that's kind of how I came to this situation or to this job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, may I respectfully congratulate you on your knowledge of history and of law, and may I put to you this principle which I believe is to be found in the law, that is to say that a court is not a historical institute. Do you know of that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've never heard that expression before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could do some research on it and find what are the limitations which are promised by that proposition. Now, could I ask you this: Do I gather that your dissatisfaction with Mr. Stewart is that he appeared to be to you reluctant to accept advice and that he was unpleasant, arrogant, and condescending? Would that sum up the ground of your dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you should add disorganised to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Disorganised. Very well, I will dutifully add that concept. Now, last question. Is this -- do you have any awareness of where Mr. Stewart is at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, if there are no other questions from the Bench, I believe it's the right time to break now. It is now time to break. I believe we should go into open session and just break immediately afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. So now we break until 10.30. We resume the hearing at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, and I will turn to the Prosecutor to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, you commented during -- perhaps we could go to private session immediately, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to private session then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, you commented --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, during the course of your testimony this morning you mentioned that at some point you had your letter translated into Serbian and you faxed the letter to Mr. Krajisnik. Do you have a date on which you faxed the letter to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes. October 19th.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge did he receive that letter personally?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I don't know if he received it that day, but I know he did receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. And so you know that Mr. Krajisnik was aware of your concerns relating to the conduct of his -- of Mr. Stewart in particular?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And I'm just going to bring to your attention the words of Mr. Krajisnik in a hearing on February the 28th, 2005, at page 9603, where Mr. Krajisnik says: "I have to say that whatever both my counsel stated here today I endorse. I do not have anything to comment, to raise in relation to the services provided by my counsel. They are very good lawyers." So I suggest to you, sir, that Mr. Krajisnik did not accept your advice about the competence of his lawyers, because not four months later he said they were very good lawyers in court before the Court. Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Are you asking me if I agree that Mr. Accepted my accept my advice? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I suggest to you he rejected your advice.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It would appear so that on that day he rejected my advice, but from what I understand from his daughter, I'm in e-mail contact with Mr. Krajisnik's daughter, that his attitude was that there was nothing he could do about it; so we'll just keep going along with it as it is. It was kind of an attitude that it was a hopeless situation, so I'll just continue with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: How long have you been in communication with his daughter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I think the first time I contacted her was maybe December of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you've been in e-mail communication ever since?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. It's not like I receive a message from her every week. I get two or three a year from her, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And do those communications relate to the trial and the appeal of his case?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And is she providing you with information as to what his strategy is in terms of his appeal and was during the course of the trial?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No. She has -- she does not get involved in the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, we know from your evidence that Mr. Krajisnik was aware of the contents of your letter. Did you send your letter to anyone else at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: In the Tribunal? What time period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Let's say -- let's start in 2004. We might go past there.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay. As I said, I had a translator from another case translate my letter, so, yeah, there was definitely someone else from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have occasion to send your letter or any other document to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I sent a letter to the Judges of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: November 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: What -- what was in your letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I believe I sent a copy of the letter I sent to Mr. Van de Vliet, his reply, my reply to him, and then a brief letter to the Judges saying that I was very concerned about the situation and that he wanted them to be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you ever get a response from the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I got a response saying that the Judges would not review what I sent them because I was not working at the Tribunal, and they were not allowed or permitted to receive information from people outside the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And what provoked you to send a letter to the Trial Chamber Judges about your impressions?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It was suggested to me that because of the response I had received from Mr. Van de Vliet that maybe someone else at the Tribunal should know about it, particularly the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Who suggested that to you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It was another Defence attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Michael Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, Mr. Mano, that you have no professional expertise in order to comment on the management or preparation of a major criminal defence case?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I would say it's not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: So you say you have experience in dealing with a major criminal defence case, and you had that experience in 2004?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: If you're asking if I have experience actually participating in the preparation of a major criminal case, the answer is no, I do not have that kind of experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you've never practice law; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I work for a law firm in America for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Three months?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Intern?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I will ask the question again you have never practice law in your life, have you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: As lawyer, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You've never practice criminal law in your life, have you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You've never taken a witness in court, have you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You've never made closing or opening argument in court have you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You've never prepared an expert for testimony, have you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: So when you joined the Defence team of Mr. Krajisnik on July the 5th, 2006, you had --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, I joined on July 6th, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: July 6th 2004. You had three months of internship at a law firm in the United States under your belt; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you described during the course of your testimony a number of particular assignments that you had to do during the course of your internship. Perhaps you could sort of go through them one by one in the order that you remember them.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the first one, as I said, was the agreement on facts between the Prosecution and the Defence. There were, I believe, two maybe three sets of facts that I was shown in the first week. After that, what would be the next thing? Maybe the next thing was preparation for cross-examination of the witness, and then I believe I started working on the expert witness testimony, and that lasted for probably several weeks, and then maybe there was another cross-examination of a witness I had to prepare for. I can't remember. And then I worked on the historical background document for several weeks, and then I believe the last thing I worked on maybe was also preparation of a witness for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: So it sounds to me that you were given specific tasks with specific goals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And how large was the team while you were on it in the summer of 2004?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah, it varied.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters ask speakers not to overlap but to make pauses between questions and answers for the sake of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. The team varied because some of the interns came and went. Some had been there before I was there. Some -- and then left before I left. Others came sometime before I left and then left after I left. I think when I first came there, besides Nicholas Stewart, Chrissa Loukas and Tatjana Cmeric, the case manager, there was also Andrej Jonovic, and Mika Dixon, and there was the other intern Thomas Derrington. There was someone named Karen Brackman [phoen] that I didn't know very well. I think I only met her on one occasion. So that was the team probably until the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was there also investigators working in the region?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I believe there was an investigator, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And there were also consultants and advisors that were available to Mr. Stewart and the other -- and Chrissa Loukas?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: What do you mean by consultants or advisors?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, for example?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: If you look at the oral argument on July 16th, the Prosecution raised Mr. Neskovic at that time; and Nicholas Stewart said that he had -- if you -- I don't want to misquote him, but it was something to the effect that he had very little contact with Mr. Neskovic and that -- because Mr. Neskovic if it's the person I'm thinking of only spoke Serbia, and Mr. Stewart did not speak Serbian that his contact with him when it did occur was through a translator and was written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But he still was advising the team; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes, but to a very limit extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did these other interns and other people working on the file have specific tasks like you did?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And they were clear tasks to them?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, in order to do a task I assume it has to be clear. I don't know how you would do a task that's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, your letter is dated the 23rd of September, 2004. When did you prepare the letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I -- I couldn't tell you exactly, but probably over the course of maybe one or two days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did you refer to any materials, notes, transcripts, documents in the preparation of your letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: At this point in time I don't remember, but -- yeah, I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did anyone assist you in the preparation of the letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did you discuss the contents of the letter before you signed it and gave it to Mr. Van de Vliet?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Discuss it with whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Anyone.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No. Not that I'm aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, when you wrote your letter the first two words in your letter are the words, "I believe."

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay. Just a second. Can I grab a copy of the letter, because I don't have one in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. I have a copy now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm just -- you can correct me if I'm wrong. I'm suggesting to you that this letter is nothing but your layman's opinion as to the quality of Nicholas Stewart's management of the Defence team at the time that you were there for three months in September -- or July through September of 2004.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree with that statement or not?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, when you in the first big paragraph say "...'average intelligent person's knowledge of the facts,'" I suppose from your testimony this morning that you've realised that that quote suggesting that those are the precise words of Mr. Stewart was inaccurate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah, you just asked me a while ago if I had any notes or documents with me. I think I did not have any notes or documents with me, so I was going by my memory of what he said in the room. I have since then reviewed the oral argument of July 16th and this is maybe slightly off, one or two words off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The Chamber can check to see how many words it's off, but why did you put it in quotes when you hadn't verified that those were his precise words?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. I shouldn't it put it in quotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But you agree it's inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It's not an accurate quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you use quotes elsewhere. At the bottom of the second page. You say about Mr. Stewart, "...stated in court, in front of the Judges, that he 'didn't know whether he,'" and then you have Krajisnik in parentheses "'was innocent or not.'" Did you look for that quote in the transcript before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, I didn't have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And I -- I can tell you that I have --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- and I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that that quote is equally inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't know. I was doing this from memory, so I have to look for it myself. If I find it, can I provide you with that information at a later date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You have nothing with you today to show that that quote attributed to Mr. Stewart in court is accurate, do you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I have nothing with me today, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And at the time that you prepared this, knowing that you were going to be handing it to the Registry and attacking Mr. Stewart, you did not take the time to verify that that quote was accurate, did you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: First of all, I was not attacking Mr. Stewart; and secondly, it wasn't a question of taking the time. I didn't have the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that all of the other quotes that you refer to could be similarly inaccurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: You can suggest that. I don't know if -- which quotes are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The minnows quote for example. You say: "I was not going to stay there. There is nothing but minnows there." Could you be mistaken about that quote?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: He did use the word minnows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But did he use it in the context you presented, sir?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: He did use it in this context.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please make pauses between questions and answers for the sake of interpretation and the record.
