utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, you're suggesting from the minnows quote that Mr. Stewart had a condescending attitude towards Mr. Gaynor and all of the other junior Prosecutors working on the case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes. Or at least towards Mr. Gaynor. I can't speak for all of the other junior Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you, sir, that Mr. Stewart was in court with Mr. Gaynor on several occasions and did the cross-examination of the witnesses that Mr. Gaynor, in fact, presented?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Why would that surprise me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You suggested that it was beneath him to go in court with junior people?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: He may have had no other option of appearing in court with Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you say on this particular day he was expressing his condescending attitude by not being in court with Ms. Loukas when Mr. Gaynor was taking a witness?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: There is no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that Mr. Stewart was in court the next four days after Mr. Gaynor took this witness on the 26th of July, 1994 -- or 2004, I'm sorry, and that Mr. Stewart was in court the next four days cross-examining -- hearing the evidence and cross-examining a big witness put on by another junior counsel, Stephen Margetts. Are you suggesting that his time was better spent in court on a witness taken by Mr. Gaynor or Ms. Loukas instead of preparing for a more significant witness?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting anything like that. I'm just telling you what he said to me when he left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And based on a passing comment which may have been a joke, you've decided to suggest that he had a condescending attitude towards all junior Prosecutors. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I didn't interpret it as a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, you gave your letter to Mr. Van de Vliet. Did he respond to you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: After you gave him the letter.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, we had a conversation in his office at that time, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did he ever send you something in writing explaining what he had done with your letter, if anything?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes. On October 4th I received a fax from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. And what did that fax say?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Just a second. Would you like me to read this or would you like a summary of it? How would you like me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Maybe you could just tell us the bottom line.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Basically he's saying that after hearing Mr. Stewart's explanation that he thought that I did not have enough time spent with Mr. Stewart to give the kind of evaluation on his performance that I had suggested and that he was not prepared at that time to deliver the letter to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And you felt that it was necessary for you to pass your letter to Mr. Krajisnik. Is it at that point that you decided to have the letter translated and faxed to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: My goal was never to -- my goal was not just to put the document in the hands of Mr. Van de Vliet. My goal was to get the letter into the hands of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And if that was the goal, why didn't you use the procedure that you ultimately succeeded in, and that is providing the information to Mr. Krajisnik in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: By myself or what are you suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You were able to have the letter translated.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah, but if I had thought of that at that time I would have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you had booked a meeting with Mr. Van de Vliet and you prepared the letter for the purposes of ensuring that you had something to bring to the meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah, because as I said, I didn't know if I was going to be able to have a long conversation with him or not. So I thought I should have something prepared in writing just in case he said, "I only have a minute with you. What do you want to say?" And I could say, "Here's the letter. Read it and get back to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you ever before preparing the letter ask Mr. Stewart for a discussion about your views relating to specific problems that had arisen, at least in your mind, during the course of your internship?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I think we covered this earlier this morning. I had raised objections several times, but after, you know, several attempts at making suggestions that were knocked down I, along with my co-workers, just gave up trying to give advice to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did you give Mr. Stewart a copy of your letter before you sent it or gave it to Mr. Van de Vliet?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And it's at least implicit from the e-mail from Mr. Van de Vliet to you that he had shared at least some of the information in your letter with Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's right. He showed him the letter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Stewart gave his reaction?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm going to read you from a transcript page from hearing transcript imagine 9599, February 28, 2005, Mr. Stewart talking on the record: "I have personally been subjected to the scurrilous attack from a former member of my team with untruthful allegations about how I spend my time, when there's an adjournment, how much work I do other than this case of which I do practically none, Your Honour." Let's adjust stop there. I suggest to you, sir, that this is a response by Mr. Stewart to your letter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I don't know if it's correct, but it could possibly be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And in respect of his statement about what he does other than work on the Krajisnik case, he says he does practically none. Aside from the one example of his going to London for one day, you have no other evidence to provide or facts to provide to suggest that he was working on other cases during the time that you were an intern?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: He actually stated in the oral argument on the 16th of July, 2004, that he kept a working practice in London and that the Krajisnik case was not the only thing he was working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did you understand that he just been put on the case less than a year before, and he was extricating himself from the practice that he had when he took over the Krajisnik case and was keeping the Trial Chamber informed of how he was using his time in that regard?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Actually, he was put on the Krajisnik case more than a year before, and I was aware that he was trying to extricate himself from his law practice in London, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But getting back to my question, you know of only one example, the trip to London for one day, that was business related?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: He made another trip to London in September when he went to Spain, he went to Spain on September 8th, and according to the e-mail I have, he was planning on spending the last day in London before returning to The Hague. I don't know exactly how long he spent in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You don't know did in London either, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how was it in September of 2007 that you came to send a fax to Mr. Krajisnik at the penitentiary enclosing your letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes. September 13, 2007 you sent him a copy of the -- of your letter.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Oh, I was asked -- apparently he had lost my earlier copy, so I was asked to send it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I think by Mr. Krajisnik himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did you -- you also mentioned that you'd had some conversation with Mr. Karganovic?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: How many times did you talk to Mr. Karganovic before September 2007 when you sent the letter to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I don't know. Steve and I are friends. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: How long have you been friends?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Since I started working at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you stay in regular contact with him over the years?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. We lost contact for a little -- sorry for the interpreters. We'd lost contact for a while but I've been more or less in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: When do you recall first discussing with Mr. Karganovic your letter of September 23rd, 2004?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It was sometime after he became case manager for Mr. Krajisnik, but I don't think I could pinpoint a date for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And what was the nature of his inquiry about the letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I think he was expressing concern about Mr. Stewart's defence, and I had mentioned my letter in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And did you help him prepare his letter of October 2007?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did he speak to you about his intention to prepare this letter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I think I stated earlier today that I knew he was going to write a letter, but I have never seen it; and I don't know the contents of it. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the accused and the appellant in these proceedings, Mr. Krajisnik, has a first-hand and probably expert knowledge of the historical background of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995? Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you have no doubt that Mr. Stewart and Mr. Krajisnik were talking on a regular basis about the case and the preparations of the case?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I don't have any first-hand knowledge of the regularity of their meeting, but I assume they did talk about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And Mr. Stewart had Mr. Krajisnik to rely on for advice as to the historical aspects of the case to the extent that he may not understand them himself, did he not?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I guess you're assuming he would listen to his advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: He had Mr. Krajisnik available to give him advice. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. He was available for that reason, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And he also had Mr. Neskovic available?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes, he was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And before making your criticism of Mr. Stewart and his lack of knowledge of the historical and political matters relating to Mr. Krajisnik's case or the case against Mr. Krajisnik, did you have occasion to review Mr. Stewart's cross-examination of the political insider witnesses like Krajisnik Witness 623 on -- who testified on the 20th through the 23rd of September, 2004?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Who was -- I'm sorry, who was the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I can't give you the name.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay. I might have actually been involved in reviewing the depositions of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. And so you would have been giving advice to Mr. Stewart on areas for cross-examination; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Generally I would type up my comments and hand them to Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. And she would pass them along to the counsel who was going to be doing the cross-examination if it wasn't her?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And so she was managing that part of the exercise, the preparation for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I don't know if I would use the word managing, but it was our -- it was my regular procedure to type up my comments and then hand them to Ms. Stewart -- or Ms. Loukas, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And in terms of other political overview witnesses that testified, Patrick Treanor the expert and his cross-examination in April 2004 by Mr. Stewart, did you have occasion to review that before you made your comments?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Not before I made my comments, but since then I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And why were you doing that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I was interested in the testimony of Mr. Treanor because I had asked Chrissa Loukas -- Chrissa Loukas on one occasion what was the foundation for allowing all of these witnesses. Mr. Krajisnik -- there was no evidence that Mr. Krajisnik had ever committed a crime, that he order someone to kill someone, for example, or that he was even present in a lot of the municipalities and locations that the Prosecution was mentioning. So I asked just a standard question any American would, American attorney would ask is what's the foundation for bringing in these witnesses. And then I asked was it Mr. Treanor, was it his testimony, and Ms. Loukas said it was not but she did not tell me what the foundation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: So notwithstanding that she said it was not, you took a look at his cross-examination by Mr. Stewart, did you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. I had already read Mr. Treanor's documents that he gave as an expert witness because I was preparing the expert witness for our client as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. And you weren't privy to any of the discussions that took place in the Defence team relating to the calling of expert witnesses during the course of Mr. Krajisnik's case, were you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: You mean before or after I was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: After you left.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: So the only thing you can testify to is that Defence was examining the possibility of expert witnesses on certain areas of the case and that you participated in part of that exercise; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about the statement of admitted facts exercise. It's my understanding that the statement of facts exercise was ongoing when you join the team on July the 5th, 2004.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And from your testimony I understand that you -- you were present at least a couple of meetings where the statement of admitted facts were discussed?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Two meetings. And you had occasion to review the proposed statement of admitted facts and to comment on the accuracy or otherwise of the statements proposed; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And my understanding of the process is that for each fact the Prosecution tendered for Defence review one or more statements of witnesses who would testify as to that fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that's correct, because sometimes there were general statements without a statement from a -- excuse me. There were general statements that the Prosecution had written that may have come from several witnesses or from -- or one line of one -- from testimony may have provided several statements from the Prosecution. It wasn't a one-to one correspondence, if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But there may be two or three witnesses testifying as to a fact or one witness testifying to as to several facts?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: And there may be one sentence that produce three or four different facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Which -- each individual fact, and that was broken down so that each individual fact in the statement could be looked at and either accept or rejected; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes. And there were also statements that were not attributed to -- you know, there were additional phrases or sentences along with those. Those were the real problems, not the statements from the witnesses but the additional things that the Prosecutors put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And the Defence could reject any statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And in fact, is it not so that sometime after the meeting on July the 9th, over that weekend a determination was made by Nick Stewart and others on the Defence team not to pursue the statement of admitted facts project any longer and require the Prosecution to call of these witnesses, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I'm glad you raised that because that's an interesting circumstance. As I said, Mr. Stewart seemed to reject my advice, but on that Friday, the 9th of July, we had one of our rather lengthy meetings at his apartment regarding the case, and the other intern -- one the other interns, Thomas Derrington, who had participated in one of the discussions with the Prosecution regarding the statements of facts said kind of off-hand that the Prosecution seemed very happy about the agreements they made, and that seemed to have a strong effect on Nicholas Stewart more than my objections that the Prosecution was possibly taking advantage of him, that he was -- that they were happy with the results; and I think that's what led him to conclude on Monday that he no longer wanted to participate in the statements of fact process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'll spare you the Prosecution's perspective, sir.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to hear it some other time though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But you do agree that on the morning of the 12th of July, 2004, Nick Stewart officially informed the Court that all discussions relating to the admitted facts for the two municipalities that had been used as the experimental ones had been discontinued and the Prosecution would be requested to prove all of the facts that it had sought to have proven by way of admitted facts; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, I don't want to press you if you have more questions, but you have been examining the witness for more than 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I apologise for that. I am almost finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I wanted to draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about a plan. I guess nobody shared with you what the Defence plan was. Is that your complaint?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: My complaint is that no one -- is not that no one shared it with me but that I wasn't aware of any plan existing, and the other interns had the same -- at least the ones I talked to, had the same feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But one interpretation is that it was never shared with the interns. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And that the plan was clearly in the -- known to Mr. Krajisnik and his Defence team of Ms. Loukas and Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: You'll have to ask them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You don't know. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Judge Meron wants to put an additional question. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, did you share your views concerning the quality of Mr. Stewart's representation with other members of the Defence team except Mr. Karganovic and, if so, how did they react?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I certainly shared it with Thomas Derrington, and with Andrej Jonovic and possibly with Chrissa Loukas as well. I know sometimes Chrissa Loukas was very stressed, so I may have shared it with her as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Regarding Ms. Loukas which was my next question, could you try to tell us the most specific discussion you had with her if you can remember on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You said today on a number occasions you said that you had the impression that she was aware of that, and she was worried about the quality of the representation. Could I hear your specific recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish I had one for you, but four years have passed. If I had written them down at the time probably I could share them too, but I can't think of any specifically right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let me turn now to the Defence of Mr. Dershowitz. I understand that the amicus curiae doesn't want to take the floor, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. So, Mr. Dershowitz, you may be allowed to take some questions, to give some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I must admit I find it quite awkward to be in all of these wires, pushing the microphone and at the same time trying to stand up and delivering in this manner, but I will try my best under, for me, unique circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, when you first joined the team, did Mr. Stewart ever sit down with you and discuss the strategy or goal of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No, did he not.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And in your presence was there ever a discussion of the strategy and goal of the Defence by Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And am I correct that you never heard a discussion as to what the Prosecutor's burden was with respect to JCE, nor a discussion of what the Defence should challenge with respect to JCE? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And am I further correct that aside from the one documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just -- I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Dershowitz. I'm just wondering about the propriety of the questions given the fact that Mr. Mano is a friendly witness to the accused. Basically we now have Mr. Dershowitz giving evidence and the witness saying yes and no, and I just object to the form of the question. Perhaps the questions could be formed a little less leading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness is a Court witness and not a Defence witness, and I think that's the criteria that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: But in any event, can you put your questions in a less leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: You indicated that you had prepared a report on experts.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It was more than a report. It was a folder full of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And did Mr. Stewart request that of you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I believe I suggested it.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Well, is the same thing true with respect to the historic background that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I suggested that to Chrissa Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: But you never had a discussion -- did you have a discussion with Mr. Stewart before you undertook that work?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No. You mean about whether I should undertake it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: In the country where I practice, it's sometimes said that one person's history is another person's current events. When you prepared the document of the history, did that cover the period from 1990 through 1992?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And was that the period the indictment?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: So by historic events, you were also including events that were relevant and material to the indictment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And I may have asked you this, but to your knowledge the only document that you had seen with respect to the legal requirements with respect to JCE was prepared solely at your request; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: You seem to be suggesting that most of the work, and I'll and we'll get to the question of preparing the cross-examination, but that most of the work that you did, you did as a self-starter, not at the behest of Mr. Stewart or anyone else in the Defence team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I don't know if I would say the word "most," but certainly a lot of the work I did was self-started.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Well, aside from preparing cross-examination material, the two other items you worked on most of the time was the -- what you call the historic background, what I call the facts relating to the case, and the preparation of the listing of persons who could be expert witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And nobody suggested to you an approach to who should be considered as expert witnesses and how it would fit into the Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And do you have any personal knowledge as to whether the document that you call the historic record and whether the document that you prepared for purposes of listing expert witnesses and whether the document that was prepared of law with respect to JCE, whether any of those documents were ever thoroughly reviewed by Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And you never received any feedback from Mr. Stewart as to the substance of any of those documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether you or anyone else on the Defence team was ever requested to prepare a historic or a document from a Defence point of view of Mr. Krajisnik's involvement for the period 1990 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It did not come up while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And with respect to your preparing witnesses for cross-examination, you mentioned that the raw data you use was depositions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Who had taken those depositions?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: They have investigators who took those in most cases, in the cases that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And those investigators, were they investigators for the Defence or were they investigators for the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: They were, I think, either investigators for the Prosecutor or some kind of Tribunal investigators, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: So you know of no raw data that you examined for purposes of preparing witnesses for cross-examination which reflected materials from a Defence point of view; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And you have no knowledge -- when you did this preparation, as far as you could tell, there was no materials that were provided to you which would indicate that it came from Mr. Krajisnik directly or anyone on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: There was one occasion where, I think, Mr. Krajisnik was asked to provide a list of questions for a witness. I did not actually see the list of questions, but I know he was asked to provide a list of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: But you didn't use that list for the purpose of preparing the materials that you would prepare for cross-examination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the guidelines for your preparing materials for cross-examination was solely to see whether there was any material in the depositions or other items that had been secured by the Prosecutor or the Tribunal which would reflect an inconsistency between that and what the witness was going to testify to?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And no idea and no materials were included which would counter the witness's testimony from a Defence point of view or a document from a Defence point of view which would aid the defendant or the Defence in questioning this witness to show that the whole level of testimony was inaccurate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Nothing that I didn't bring myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And what you brought yourself was knowledge that you had, not knowledge that you secured from Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Dershowitz, may I ask you to be less leading, because I see you are going back to very much leading when putting questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: I apologise. I will try not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Court with, I think -- are we in private session? You were asked to examine a last sentence-the last full sentence on page 3 which says: "That statement alone should be convincing evidence to anyone that Mr. Stewart should not be left to handle the case," and in response to an inquiry from the Tribunal you said you should have said "that and everything else." Could you please explain what you meant by "everything else"?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Well, the concerns that I expressed in this letter, his lack of knowledge, his refusal to take advice from anyone, his lack of personal interest in the outcome, the combination of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Also when you were asked a question by the Tribunal about that he took little personal interest in the outcome, I think you indicated you didn't have specific things in mind, but you seem to have had some general impressions in mind. Can you explain what you had in mind when you made that statement?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah. He had said things to me either when I was riding in his car or when I had time to talk to him alone that suggested to me that it really wasn't important whether he won or lost -- whether he would win or lose the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Were there any other comments that he made that fit into that general category?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I'm sure there were. That wasn't an exact quote. I don't remember his words exactly. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Well, putting aside his exact words, are you sure of the impression that he conveyed to you and your reaction to his questions?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: You had been asked by Mr. Kremer whether you were aware of a comment made by Mr. Krajisnik -- let me strike that. You were asked by Mr. Kremer that if Mr. Krajisnik indicated in February of 2005 that he was satisfied with the Defence, that would indicate that he rejected your advice. If you also understood that Mr. Krajisnik had suggested that he want to be self-represented and that if he was self-represented it would not make things any worse, would that indicate to you that he did recognise what you were saying as having validity?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: It would seem to indicate that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions with respect to the substance -- the accuracy of your exact quotations, and you indicated they may not have been accurate, but can you tell us in substance whether each of the items that's contained in that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again, Mr. Dershowitz. I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Dershowitz. I rise to object simply because I don't understand what, if any, connection this has with JCE. Mr. Dershowitz has a very specific function, and he asked two questions about JCE and everything else is -- are questions that should have been asked by Mr. Dershowitz, and he knows this; and I just stand to object on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: I would love the opportunity to respond on that, Your Honour, and that is the conviction here was solely on the basis of JCE. To the extent that counsel did not prepare, did not prepare in general, and as I think this witness has indicated certainly did not prepare at all with an understanding that JCE could be the subject of the conviction; and it was the subject of the conviction, the lack of preparation, the lack of doing any work with respect to JCE is, in my view, indispensable to a determination of ineffectiveness of counsel. Ineffectiveness of counsel is not in the abstract. It ties into the specific charges and more so to the specific charges for which a defendant was convicted. So to prepare for A when a defendant is convicted of B is in my mind irrelevant. You must prepare for what the defendant could be convicted of, and here the evidence seems to suggest no preparation for purposes of JCE. So it's all relevant with respect to JCE. And I only have about three more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: All right. Put the three more questions but try to be more focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Again my question is you were asked whether or not the quotations you made reference to were specifically accurate and whether the quotation marks should have been around that, and I ask you whether those quotations are in substance accurate.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: In substance they are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And you did it from memory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: You were asked two other questions by Mr. Kremer. One is whether Mr. Stewart had access to Mr. Krajisnik for securing factual materials. Do you have any knowledge as to whether Mr. Stewart ever secured factual information from Mr. Krajisnik, except for the one example that you gave where he was asked to provide questions for cross-examination? Were you aware whether or not in any of the conversations he ever had with Mr. Krajisnik whether he ever asked him facts responsive to allegations that were made by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: The same thing with respect to Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Neskovic, where there was an indication that he was available. Do you have any personal knowledge as to whether Mr. Stewart ever secured information from him and ever use that information?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: No. Actually, the -- quite the contrary. If you look at Mr. Stewart's oral argument from July 16, 2004, when the Prosecution raised Mr. Neskovic's name saying that he had billed the Tribunal for some incredibly high number of hours, Mr. Stewart said, "I wasn't aware of that." And then he went on to say that Mr. Neskovic is in Bosnia, that he only speaks Serbian, that Mr. Stewart is in The Hague, and he only speaks English, and that the few times he had contact with him were via a translator and written material.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And the final subject is Mr. Kremer asked you questions about the proposed statement of facts and said that the normal procedure is to have certain witness -- testimony from witnesses indicating that they would support the statement. Do you have any idea whether simply because there is an allegation that a witness will testify to something means, one, that that witness is credible; two, that that testimony is admissible, and I can go on.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a good question. And also as I said, the Prosecution elaborated on what the witnesses said. So there were a lot of things that were objectionable about the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: So it wasn't just the substance but also the procedure by which they were going to support it may have been able to have been challenged; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE MANO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we conclude -- well, Judge Meron first, and then I may have a couple of questions myself, but please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just one question to Mr. Dershowitz. We know that the witness worked for three months in the Tribunal as an intern. Now, it may very well be that the question of joint criminal enterprise was elaborated after that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: What is in fact the significance that we should draw from the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. What is the significance of the fact that Mr. Mano cannot testify to anything he remembers about joint criminal enterprise studies having being prepared in that span of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer I think if you take that coupled with a number of other things, it raises a question. It certainly doesn't solve the question. But if you have a period of time where the only one who had prepared materials was a member of the team requested by Mr. Mano, if you add to that a statement that was made by Ms. Loukas at one point in time which said that the priorities of the Defence was not to do certain types of technical legal research, and then depending upon what Mr. -- what the next case manager says, it may simply be sufficient to raise a question as to whether there was ever -- that Mr. Stewart ever engaged in preparing for joint criminal enterprise. And the only way you'll ever have an answer to that question probably with any degree of definity is whether Mr. Stewart testifies. When you take those three pieces and put it together there is a strong inference that that work had never been done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Following on this question, Mr. Dershowitz, would you in light of the limited time spent by the witness with the Defence team and of the fact that he has been assigned specific tasks as he has stated before, with a limited goal, would you allow for the possibility that the witness was not given more substantive tasks, was not associated in the preparation of the defence simply because perhaps the lead counsel did not trust him enough in light of his lack of expertise, legal expertise and legal practice, and didn't want to associate him, not withstanding his wish to be associated?

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, without a doubt that may be the case, but when you allow for two witnesses to testify on the narrow question, you have to control whatever information you can from those two witnesses. There are other witnesses who I believe may be necessary to get a full picture. I completely agree you will not get a full picture from these two witnesses, but there are Mr. Stewart, Ms. Loukas, other people, and you know -- but that's not -- that's not within my -- my realm. I agree with you completely that you can draw certain conclusions, certain limited conclusions, but you cannot draw conclusions as to everything from witnesses who were not there for the full period of time. But again, I think the reason for the hearing is because there is enough within these documents to suggest some problem, and exploring them increases the fact that there is a problem. It didn't fully answer the problem, and that's -- that's my view on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Mano, would you kindly correct my impression in case it's wrong, as well as it may be, that is I gained the impression from your evidence that the briefing notes on historical matters which you prepared were limited really to a narration of current events over one or two years, that they did not go into prior matters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I provided the background for the conflict going back to before World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How far did that background note extend into the past? Would you say ten years or hundreds of years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As I said, I started with the background that led up to World War II, so that would have encompassed a period of time probably of 60 or 70 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: One more question just to -- Mr. Mano, to clarify one issue which perhaps was not clear through the debate we had now. You were saying you were given task of preparing witnesses for cross-examination, but from some of the intervention I got you preparing materials to be used for cross-examination. What exactly was the task you assigned in the preparation for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. As I said, I was usually given depositions or something like depositions, statements by witnesses; and I was asked to review the statements and try to find contradictions or obvious things that could not be correct within those statements, and then I would type out my own observations, and I would hand those to Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Well, this concludes the examination of Witness Mano. Mr. Mano, you may be excused and accompanied out of the courtroom. We go back to public hearing now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So before closing this morning's session, may I raise one issue. The Appeals Chamber received this morning a request by Mr. Krajisnik to file, in relation to the hearing on Wednesday, next Wednesday, to file Radovan Karadzic statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Of course the Appeals Chamber will have to decide on this, but may I ask the Prosecution if they have any comment on this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have people meeting, discussing it. I will meet with them during the recess and hopefully will be in the position to file something today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. So we defer this to the afternoon in order to enable the Appeals Chamber to make a decision later on. The hearing is now adjourned. We reconvene at 2.00 for the examination of the Witness Karganovic. The hearing is adjourn. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.49 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon everybody. We resume our hearing. At the outset let me thank the Prosecution for the response we received on the request of Mr. Krajisnik to -- leave to file a document under Rule 92 ter. The Appeals Chamber will consider the issue and will give an answer, announce its decision before the end of the afternoon, before the end of the hearing. Now we can perhaps proceed -- Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission perhaps it would be a good idea before you reach your decision with respect to the Prosecution's response that in my own name and Mr. Dershowitz's name he present additional reasons which would be useful to you in making your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I consulted my colleagues. Yes, of course this can be done, but I wouldn't like to open a long debate now; and it should be understood it's the expense of the Defence time if they want to add some reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just Mr. Krajisnik asked me to explain and to address one paragraph in the response which says that Mr. Krajisnik provides no reason as to why it would be, you know, compatible with the interest of justice. And the reason he had wanted to have this done by a document is because he is pro se, and he was concerned about his capacity and ability to be able to ask the questions in an area that he thinks is significant as well as it could be done by a document, and he thought that since Mr. Kremer can cross-examine, Mr. Nicholls intends to cross-examine, and I have been given permission to examine, that between those three the Court will have enough of a face-to-face of Mr. Karadzic to be able to make the judgement as to his credibility. I just wanted to explain -- he wanted me to explain that in legal terms, that's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Any reaction on this just by the Prosecution just to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Our concern is the unfairness of the document going in as a 92 ter statement solely without eliciting what Mr. Krajisnik thinks are important aspects of the statement. We're on notice that he may testify as to all of those points. Some of them are not very detailed or elaborate and basically deal with all of the testimony, and for us to be effective in our cross-examination we need to know through the mouth of the witness what he's saying, why he's saying it, and how he's saying it in order to be able to properly challenge both his credibility in terms of making those statements and also the content of them. So that would be my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Well, the Appeals Chamber will take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes. My attention is drawn on the one point made by Mr. Dershowitz when you said a moment ago that you have given permission to examine. You mean re-examine after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Correct. I want to make sure the procedure is clear to everyone. Well, we will take into account -- the Appeals Chamber will take into account the consideration just made by the parties. I don't know whether the amicus wants to say something on this specific point made by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I have nothing really to add. The document obviously has a value from the Chamber's view and indeed from counsel's view, but it can't be evidence other than -- insofar as it is given from the witness box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry, what do you mean by that, Mr. Nicholls? If the document is admitted as evidence under 92 ter, it's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that it should be admit as evidence. I'm saying that it's useful from our point of view in that we have it or counsel have it, but obviously he have must be given from the witness box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Nicholls, I have to explain the procedure then. If a statement is admitted under 92 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, that document is evidence. Of course, it will be taken into account together with the cross-examination. It takes place -- it is in lieu of examination-in-chief, but it has the same value of examination-in-chief, and of course we have to consider in light of the cross-examination, the re-examination, but it's part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then in my capacity as amicus, I have no submissions to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify. Under 93 ter, there is no indication of interest of justice. Under 89(F) there is an indication of an interests of justice. They are two different Rules. I just wanted to highlight that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We know the Rules, Mr. Dershowitz.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Better than I do, I'm sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So I believe now we can reserve in the decision on the request. We can proceed to examining Witness Karganovic. Can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Just before we start, Mr. President, I just have one question that arises out of our examination and cross-examination of the witness this morning; and I would raise the question as to whether or not Mr. Dershowitz, to the extent that he has any JCE questions, should not go after the Bench, and I be given the last opportunity to ask questions of Mr. Karganovic subject to the Chamber asking questions. I just say from my experience this morning I think the process is entirely unfair to have Mr. Dershowitz asking questions of a friendly witness -- of a witness friendly to Mr. Krajisnik who Mr. Krajisnik who is proposing, who the Chamber has chosen to call to be asked to basically rehabilitate or attempt to rehabilitate the witness through leading questions after cross-examination. That's my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I see my colleagues have also this view. Probably it's -- we should proceed this way. So have Mr. Dershowitz taking the floor before the Prosecutor. And of course understanding that Mr. Dershowitz will limit himself to JCE issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection. I just wanted to make sure that I'm using Mr. Nicholls' time, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So can we have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- Mr. Karganovic. Can you please read the solemn declaration that the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Karganovic. You may now be seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So could you please tell the Court your full name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Stefan Karganovic. I was born on June 16, 1950. *JUDGE POCAR: Thank you. Which is your address?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: My address in Holland is Usselinexstraat 60, Den Haag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us what education you have and give us a brief list of your previous occupation and your current occupation.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My education is I went to the University of Chicago in the United States. I have a degree in philosophy. I went to Indiana University Law school and graduated there. I worked in some legal capacities and also had a private businesses in the 1980s. I also worked as an interpreter and a translator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Karganovic, the Court has ask you to testify in the appeal proceedings in the case of the Prosecutor against Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: As it is the Court itself that has requested your attendance, you will be first asked questions by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And as I am presiding here, I will begin the questioning myself, following questions by other Judges. You may then be asked questions by Mr. Krajisnik, the Defence Mr. Dershowitz, and the Prosecution, and the amicus curiae if he wants to do so. Specifically, we will be asking you questions as to what you know about the workings of Mr. Krajisnik's Defence team during the trial and about the conduct of former counsel, Nicholas Stewart, in relation to that trial.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. May I just note that on the screen I do not see anything. It would perhaps be helpful if I could also follow the questions and the answers there. Ah, yes. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Before I put you questions, one small thing. I asked you your address.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Do you want the address to remain in the record, or you want to have it redacted.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the time being I suppose that is my official address, although when I go to Belgrade I -- I can live at my aunt's house. I could give you the address there. If there is a point to it I would be happy to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: No, the problem is that since the hearing is public if you want to have it public or not, the address. You don't mind.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Thank you. So now I would ask the -- the usher to present the witness with Exhibit AD2, which is a confidential exhibit; and so before putting questions that would relate to that exhibit, I will ask the registrar to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Karganovic, this document, as you see the statement of October 16, 2007.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You want a moment to familiarise yourself with the document or you don't need that?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I wrote it, I think I'm familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You're familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: There's only one correction I would like to make. In paragraph one, the years should be moved one forward. There was a typographical mistake, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Paragraph one.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So it's from April of 2005 to May of 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So first can you confirm that you wrote this statement in.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I note that at paragraph three, four lines from the end, the word "Stewart" has been cross out by hand and replace by Loukas. Could you enlighten us as to which one of these names is correct, to replace?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Loukas. I again made a typographical error, and I corrected it by hand, and I initialled the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So with that change --

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- can you confirm that the statement represents the truth to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The statement in B/C/S certainly does. As far as the translation is concerned, I can only trust that it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's well enough. Can you enlighten us now as to whether you submitted the facts and your concerns contained in the statement to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I -- to be quite proper, I submitted it to Mr. Krajisnik, and I believe that it was Mr. Krajisnik who then submitted it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So if you don't -- so you did not submit it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not directly send it to the Chamber, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So can you explain to us why you chose not to present this -- these facts during the trial?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is a fair question. It never occurred to me, to be quite honest with you, Your Honour. I suppose when it is all over then your impressions come together and you form a more coherent picture. During the trial you're very busy. You don't have so much time for thinking. It just never occurred to me to do that during the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So you thought of submitting these facts only after the trial had ended.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And you don't think at any moment before the end of the trial to -- to submit facts of this kind to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, I note that according to your statement, you worked in Mr. Krajisnik's Defence team from April 2005 to May 2006.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: According to the correction you made to the dates.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: In paragraph six, however, you state you were going with Mr. Stewart to see Mr. Krajisnik in UN Detention Unit in autumn 2005. Can you explain the dates? Has that date to be corrected as well or -- was it autumn 2006 or does it remain autumn 2005?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: That is in which paragraph, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph six.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a little bit confused. It should have been 2000 -- now I'm completely confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Because if you move the dates in paragraph one.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: What we do for the same dates for the rest of the statement.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not think this has to be moved forward. This is probably -- okay. If we're talking about the autumn, it should be 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So this date would stand?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. Yes. Yes, because I left the team in March or April of 2006, two or three months before the trial was over. That was in 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You say you left the team now in March or April 2006.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: But in paragraph one it would be until May 2006. Which is the correct date?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me take another look. May. All right. Probably May. I'm not entirely certain of the date. It was before Mr. Krajisnik began to testify. So it may have been May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There are several other paragraphs with dates.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can we go through them and try to see whether the dates are correct or have to be --

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- or have to be considered in light of what you said in paragraph one. In paragraph two you speak about April 2004. It should be April 2005.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's correct. That should be easy to correct. What about paragraph five where you're speaking about autumn 2005.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's the year when I started working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: In that same paragraph it says May 2005.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph seven you mean, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: No, paragraph five. Fifth line. Third line on page two. "It is only May 2005 that the --"

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. "It is only May --" I think that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: The same would apply, I guess, two lines below, to the late autumn 2005.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Then in paragraph six you have a date summer 2005.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Which I again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Again correct.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: -- would say is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Beginning of paragraph seven, first line, you say May 2005.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Again I think is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And I think that's all.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's all. So at least we have tried to clarify the dates in the document. Now, one issue related to dates again. Amicus curiae has argued that Ms. Loukas resigned in July 2005. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly would agree that she left the team in July of 2005. I -- I'm not sure when she technically tendered her resignation or when her resignation is dated, but I do know that she remained for a couple of weeks and to break in Mr. Josse who had been appointed to replace her as co-counsel. So I'm not quite sure during those couple of overlapping weeks that she was still technically still co-counsel or not. I just didn't see any documents that would confirm that one way or another, but she remain physically until the break that year, which began in late May -- late July 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Indeed the correction in the dates explains some of the contradictions that I noticed in your statement, so I don't have to go to that. Let me ask you another question now.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If you go to paragraph three, you describe the Defence team's work as an improvisation.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you exemplify the basis on which you reached this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the time at least that I joined the team, we did not have any clear plan according to which we were working or at that time when I joined reacting to the Prosecution's evidence, and later of course our task became organising our own defence on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf. So it seemed that we were lurching from one crisis to another, from one emergency to another, and we often had to ask for extensions of time because we did not really have a clear idea of what we wanted to do next, and we were not sure if we were prepared for whatever was coming next. In terms of the Defence case, I think the improvisation element became particularly prominent because there was no clear pattern that I could see in calling witnesses or specific criteria by which we would select Defence witnesses to rebut a specific contention of the Prosecution or to help establish some thesis by the Defence. So there was no consistent, well-thought-out plan underlying what we were doing and that's my definition of an improvisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: What were exactly the tasks to which you were assigned within the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a dual task so to speak because I'm a B/C/S speaker. So a large portion of my duties had to do with interpretation and translation. Interpretation, obviously accompanying Mr. Stewart or Ms. Loukas or Mr. Josse to the Detention Unit to talk to Mr. Krajisnik or talk to him here, or translation. There was a lot of material that was generated by Mr. Krajisnik in B/C/S which needed to be translated into English for the benefit of his counsel. There was also quite a bit of documentation that was coming in from the investigators in the field in Bosnian which needed to be turned into English for the benefit of counsel. So that was one significant part of it. Related to that was my presence in the courtroom to serve as liaison between the defendant and counsel. Beyond that I had the task of organising documents as they were needed, bringing them to counsel. We had an office rented on the premises of the Dutch Bar Association where the bulk of our files were located. There was also a closet here where some of the most frequently used ones were being kept, but I tried to keep track of where things were and to locate them and bring them to the attention of -- of counsel as needed, assemble dossiers, so to speak, of documents that were pertinent to a particular witness or subject and so on and so forth. Also, I had the task of liaising with potential witnesses in the former Yugoslavia for a while. Then that job was taken over by another person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So it means that you say you were in the position to follow everything that happen within the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You could say that, but perhaps "everything" is -- is a very broad concept. We had staff meetings generally once a week where we would all assemble, or most of us would assemble, and we would talk about pending tasks and things of that nature; but there were some elements of should I call it confidentiality or of private interaction between Mr. Stewart and Ms. Loukas while she was on the team, and later on the same pattern continue with Mr. Josse, which I thought was perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Let me come to some specific questions. In paragraph five you speak of disagreements within the Defence team as to which witnesses should be called. Now, between who did these disagreements exist and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. The disagreements existed fundamentally between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Stewart. Mr. Krajisnik had practically all times his agenda, which witnesses would be the most suitable at any given time to be called. Mr. Stewart had his ideas, and harmonising these divergent approaches was not always easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: On a related note, in the same paragraph, paragraph five, you say that the Defence called only 20 witnesses as opposed to the 200 called by the Prosecution. Could you explain how, if at all, this relates to the conduct of Mr. Stewart? Was his decision.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the obvious answer to Your Honour's question is that he was lead counsel and in overall in charge of planning and conducting the defence. So in the final analysis it was choices that he made in that capacity that resulted in so many witnesses being called. It's a separate question whether these decisions were wise or unwise, practical or not; but that's a value judgement, but in his capacity he's the one who call the shots. Of course the fact that Mr. Krajisnik testified and took up a couple of weeks of Defence time also reduced the number of Defence witnesses who could be called. So that had an influence over it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Let me move on to paragraph six.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There you allege that Mr. Stewart admitted that, I'm quoting: "... had no idea about how to mount the defence." In paragraph nine you say more broadly the Defence team did not have a plan for the defence. Is it your claim that none of the members of the team, so no the team, not only Mr. Stewart, had a plan for the defence?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: That is a very good question. If I can focus on paragraph six first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Is Your Honour referring to the interlude in the Defence unit -- I mean in the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Well, there I'm simply quoting what Mr. Stewart said. It was said in the presence of Mr. Josse. One may take it for whatever it's worth. As far as paragraph nine is concerned, you're correct. I put it more broadly there. I speak of the Defence team. Perhaps in my mind the Defence is identified, personified by Mr. Stewart only in the sense that he was the person who was making overall and final decisions, and also in his interactions with Mr. Krajisnik insisted very adamantly that he had to be ultimately in charge. So perhaps I could have been more precise in -- in that paragraph, but now that I look at this again I would say that I meant basically the person who was running the show, Mr. Stewart. That doesn't mean that other members of the Defence team did not have their own ideas, but number one, they were not nearly as qualified to venture ideas of this nature as an experienced barrister and Queen's counsel as Mr. Stewart. Of course it would not have hurt, perhaps, for lead counsel to talk to the members of his team and hear some suggestions and ideas; but for one reason or another we never really had any team discussions on strategic issues, what is to be done. Insofar as we had discussions, it was how to accomplish something that was already decided that needed to be done. Tactical rather than strategic, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Let know now turn your attention to the issue of expert witnesses that you mentioned in paragraph nine of your statement.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You stated Mr. Stewart did not think expert witnesses would clarify the issues of the case.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us specifically why Mr. Krajisnik -- if and why Mr. Krajisnik disagreed with Mr. Stewart in this regard?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Mr. Krajisnik very strongly disagreed with Mr. Stewart on this point. He disagreed in the first place, and I can only try to convey to you what I heard from him verbally. Mr. Krajisnik would ultimately be the best person to answer your question, but from what he said, he complained that the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: But I understand you were translating and bringing to Mr. Stewart, so --

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Exactly what I want to know you heard --

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... certainly, certainly. That's what I'm going to focus on because I don't want to try to read anybody's thoughts, especially a person who is available to answer questions. But Mr. Krajisnik would point out over and over again that the Prosecution brought so many expert witnesses, I think five or six or something like that; and he thought from his intelligent layman's point of view that it was very odd that in a case of this high profile and complexity the Defence would not respond in the same manner, bring one expert witness to deal with the findings and allegations of each of the Prosecution's expert witnesses. He simply could not grasp why that would not be done. And it was even more difficult for him to understand that given the fact that after the number of years that he has spent here, he saw the way other trials were being conducted, and he noticed the obvious, namely that in the vast majority of the cases it was standard practice for the Defence to bring expert witnesses depending on whatever they wanted to prove or refute, but it was standard practice.
