So he simply could not understand why that was not being done in his case. So his starting position was that we should -- it should be one-on-one. The Prosecution had -- they had a military expert, a media expert, a demographic expert, an expert on the destruction of cultural monuments. I don't recall them all, but there were about five or six, and he wanted us to respond tit for tat. When Mr. Stewart did not agree to that, Mr. Krajisnik reduced his demands to two. He said: "Okay. Let's have a demographic expert because population movement is a very important issue in my case. And also, let us at least have a legal expert or constitutional expert who could look at the government structure of the Republika Srpska and inform the Chamber about what my position was within those structures and what I could and could not do in terms of what I was being charged with in the indictment." That didn't fly either, so Mr. Krajisnik, in his bargaining style, dropped the legal expert and he said, "Okay. We must have the demographic expert because that is absolutely a key issue in the case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I understand that a demographic expert was identified.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: In the person of Dr. Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And was contact as a potential, but was not called in.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, she was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now was it a decision of Mr. Stewart not to call her in and if it is so, for what reasons did Mr. Stewart not call her in?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was essentially in charge of their interaction because Professor Radovanovic I guess doesn't speak enough English to communicate directly; so I have that e-mail correspondence. They exchanged about five or six letters about her possible appearance, and Mr. Stewart, I -- I really hate to use emotionally charged words because it's not very objective, but I have to use the word, grudgingly went along with the idea of looking into the possibility of engaging Professor Radovanovic. So he sent her a letter through me asking her what she thinks that she could do. She responded, and I remember that the first letter or two were rather frosty, because Mr. Stewart's inquiry, not that he meant it that way. I think having grown up in the United States, it's not Great Britain but it's close enough, I have a much better idea of the British mentality than somebody in Serbia. So he didn't mean it that way but it came across that way, that he was being supercilious, just snotty and not really respecting her work and her contribution sufficiently. Unfortunately it came across that way. It wasn't meant that way. So she responded in a frosty way. So this whole correspondence really did not get off the ground the right way. And then it went on for a few more letters and then it died down. Mr. Stewart simply decided not to call her or to do anything more in relation to the subject of expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I understand. Let me come to another set of questions. Before writing your statement, did you at any point discuss the content of this statement with anybody?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: In particular, did you discuss the -- you did not discuss it with Mr. Mano.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Absolutely. I might add that I was aware that Mr. Mano also had misgivings about the conduct of the trial, but I did not discuss my specific misgivings or the content of my statement with him, nor did he discuss it with me, his own with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I have some more issues to deal with you concerning the trial. Were you aware that Mr. Stewart negotiated a set of agreed facts with the Prosecution during the pre-trial stage.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: In July 2004.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not involved in that. That was before I joined the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And you were not aware that it had happen?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware that agreed facts is a procedure that exists here, and I might have assumed that that was done in this case as well, but I had nothing to do with the process by which that was accomplished in this particular case; and I have no knowledge about what these agreed facts were ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Another question I would like to put to you. You personally know Mr. Mano.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know him virtually. I think that would be a better way of putting it than personally, because just as I arrived here and joined Mr. Krajisnik's team, he was leaving. So we overlapped for a couple of days. And I do remember that before he left to go to Japan he invited all the team members, including me, to a Japanese restaurant. So that was the only significant social contact that I with him there at that time. After --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So you mean Mr. Mano left the Tribunal in April 2005?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: He -- he left shortly after I arrived. I -- we did not overlap for very long. I met him in the Defence room. We were introduced. We were both from the United States; and we chatted, and we exchanged pleasantries when we ran into each other, but we did not really socialise to any great extent while here. We did go out to this Japanese restaurant, after which we exchanged e-mail addresses and we occasionally corresponded, and he would occasionally call me from Japan, which I took as an expression of perhaps his loneliness in a foreign culture. And he would, you know, talk to me about his job there, which was teaching English, some issues that he had with his family, with his brother in the United States, and so on and so forth. And after that the first time that I saw him was today. As I was leaving for lunch, he was leaving as well, so we just said hello to each other and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You said Mr. Mano invited all the team members to a Japanese restaurant.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stewart participate in the dinner?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He did not participate. It was the support staff that he invited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: In the limited time you overlapped with Mr. Mano, could you get any impression at least on how Mr. Mano and Mr. Stewart interacted between them?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: While I was there I did not see anything wrong. No signs of friction between them, so I have nothing special to report in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can I ask you if you and Mr. Mano ever discussed Mr. Stewart's conduct as counsel?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Over the time since we last saw each other here after he left and I arrived, by telephone. He would call me. I know that he was close, again by telephone, with Mr. Krajisnik's daughter Milica, and that he would often call her and chat with her. So he did inquire about how the trial was going. In his questions and inquiries there was a great deal of concern that was evident about Mr. Krajisnik and how he would fare in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So you discussed Mr. Stewart's conduct after he had left.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Not when you were together here.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we had no reason to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And I understand it was Mr. Mano who took the initiative to contact you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He would always call me from Japan. I never called him. But I enjoyed talking to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And did you discuss to take any action when discussing on the phone or by mail you had concern about the conduct of Mr. Stewart? Did you discuss the need to take action in that respect?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mano had told me that he already taken some action. He told me that while he was here before I arrived, he had noticed some things that had concerned him in the conduct of Mr. Stewart and that he had written a letter. I don't know now whether that letter was written to Mr. Krajisnik or to the Registry detailing these concerns. And he also told me that this letter was accompanied with a request, I believe, that it be shown to Mr. Krajisnik, translated into B/C/S, first of all, because he is American born, and I don't believe that he really speaks B/C/S. So he wrote it in English. So -- and he requested that it be translated into B/C/S and passed on to Mr. Krajisnik as an expression of his concern, but that -- while that was ultimately done, I think, the Registry showed the letter to Mr. Stewart and gave him an opportunity to write a letter of rebuttal. So that's what I know about his concerns in this area. I also know that Mr. Krajisnik, from what he told me, that Mr. Krajisnik would call him occasionally for the holidays and so on and so forth, and Mr. Mano, I think, does have a limited knowledge of Serbian. And also Mr. Krajisnik's daughter is very fluent in English, so he was able to, I think, communicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... all this information you're giving now comes from Mr. Mano or you have this information from other sources as well?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: It comes from Mr. Mano.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Exclusively?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had no other source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: When did you exactly learn of Mr. Mano's letter? When was that?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I cannot give you an exact time, but it was during the period after his departure or his return to Japan and now. So talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: But how long could have been, because you are saying -- you said earlier he left a few -- short time after you joined.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You joined in April 2005.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So how late did you learn of this letter?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: One week? One month?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, much more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Three months? One year?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: A couple of months, I think, but not one week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So it could have been in the fall of --

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly, possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, during the summer of 2005.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Well, I see Judge Meron has a question for you. I pass him the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Karganovic, thank you for your statement today. You are involved in this case as an assistant to Mr. Krajisnik; right.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Today you are a witness --

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: For the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So we are today in sort of a dual capacity witness for us and assistant. Now, this statement, your written statement, I would like to understand a little bit better whose idea was it to right it? Was --

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was my idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It was your idea. Not Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Not Mr. Mano's.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, certainly not Mr. Mano's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But the information which you include in this statement in response to the President you pointed to -- did I understand you correctly that the information itself came from Mr. Mano?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. The information that I -- that I put in my statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It contains my observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It's your -- so what was the information which you obtain from Mr. Mano in reply?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: About Mr. Mano's concerns and the letter that Mano had written before I even arrived back in The Hague about Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But the information in the statement is your information.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Time wise, it covers the period of my tenure as case manager and has nothing to do with Mr. Mano or his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You were a case manager from April of 2004 to May 2005.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: We corrected the years. Move one year forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Five and six.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now, these concerns which you expressed in the statement, Mr. Karganovic, are of course very serious concerns.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: During the time when you were a member of the Defence team did you express them to anyone or just sat on them for a long period of time?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did discuss some of these concerns, and they were shared, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: With Kelly Pitcher a young lady who was an assistant on our team, and she was in fact in charge of that office that we had on the premises of the Dutch Bar Association. So we had discussions about the direction in which the defence was going, how things were handled, and so on and so forth. I also had conversations about this with Ms. Loukas, because she was very concerned throughout the period when my tenure coincided with the last period of her role as co-counsel, and she expressed quite a few concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Did you ever share these concerns with Mr. Stewart himself?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Because with all due respect for the gentleman there, I -- I think that there was a barrier, let me put it that way, that Mr. Stewart constructed a filter. Let me use a gentler word. There was a filter. And while we could talk about many, many things both case related and non-case relate, there was a preserve, if you will, that he kept to himself as his exclusive precinct whereas lead counsel he alone had complete control, and he would not brook any contradiction. That goes without saying, but he would not even encourage or -- or allow anybody intruding with suggestions. So that may be characteristic of another legal system, namely in Great Britain, that is not so familiar to me. In America people discuss everything in an office, and even people in leadership positions encourage their -- their staff to come up with ideas and to talk about things and kick ideas around, try to come -- come up with a better solution. But in -- here we are talking about a different tradition, and I'm not going to judge it. That's just the way I found it. And I did not feel comfortable approaching Mr. Stewart even on a one to one basis, having coffee with him and saying, "Hey, Nicholas, what do you think about this? Is this the right way to go?" He created an atmosphere that you did not feel comfortable doing that. On the other hand, we had a very good, amicable relationship going beyond the office and office issues. So if that sounds like that a paradox to you, maybe this, but that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So the most senior person with whom you say -- with whom you share your concern about the quality of representation which Mr. Krajisnik received was Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it was reciprocal. It was a two-way street. She also shared her concerns with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Does your statement state clearly that you stated these concerns to Ms. Loukas, because you do mention her a number of times. I was not quite clear that you did it.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I did not say that. I'm not quite sure. I don't think I did, but I'm saying it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Karganovic, I have two questions --

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: -- to ask. The first one is you left the Defence team before the end of the work. What did you do in the meantime? Did you stay in contact with the member of the Defence team? This is the first question.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: The second point is the Prosecution contend that you were not really involved in putting false allegation to a key Prosecution witness, Milorad Davidovic, during the cross-examination at the trial.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Would you please enlighten us more on this point? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. As to your first question, you mean what did I do after that, after I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the question? After I left the Defence team, my mother, my cousin, and I went to Serbia, and we spent the summer there. As for the second question, Mr. Davidovic was a Prosecution witness who was built as a very important Prosecution witness because he may some very serious allegations about Mr. Krajisnik. He was a former functionary of the Federal Yugoslav Interior Ministry, meaning the police, and then he was a functionary of the Republika Srpska Interior Ministry, I believe, in Bijeljina. Mr. Krajisnik's investigators in Bosnia came up with some derogatory information about Mr. Davidovic. There was an allegation that Mr. Davidovic, while he occupied a position of power in Bijeljina during the war, extorted money and goods from a person there, an individual. I believe she was a doctor. I -- I think so. I'm not quite sure. I will have to refresh my memory. So the investigators who were working for Mr. Krajisnik suggested that we look into that and find out if there was any truth to those allegations, and Ms. Loukas told me to call this individual in -- at that time I think in Sarajevo or around Sarajevo, and to inquire if there was any truth in those allegations. I did so. We had a friendly conversation, and I passed on to the doctor the suggestion that he [sic] and his family may have been abused by Mr. Davidovic during the conflict, and that was the night. And I accepted the answer that I received, passed on the results of the conversation to Ms. Loukas and that was it. The following day or a few days later the Prosecution said in court that, which was perfectly true, this doctor received a call from me making these inquiries. I only acted pursuant to direction from Mrs. Loukas, Ms. Loukas. I did not make that call on my own, of course, and it was strictly to elicit information that co-counsel thought would be valuable in the case. It was conducted in a polite, professional way and that was it. I nothing to do with the merits of the allegations. I did not have -- I did not generate this information. It was passed on to us. And my task on behalf the Defence team was only to verify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: It is the case that no more questions from the Bench. I wonder whether it would be appropriate to break now because otherwise we have to break in 15 minutes, and perhaps we may have the time to discuss the other issue in between during the break. So perhaps we break now, and we -- we reconvene in, say, 25 minutes. So 20 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing, and -- I'm sorry. I remind the parties we are private session dealing with document AD2, and I will give the floor to Mr. Krajisnik to cross-examine the -- the witness for a total of 45 minutes, but then of course we have Mr. -- well, you can divide the time if Mr. Dershowitz wishes, but there will be 10 additional minutes for Mr. Dershowitz on JCE as agreed. So please, Mr. Krajisnik, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Karganovic.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: How do you do, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In your statement you make a number of observations with respect to Mr. Stewart's work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber dealt with that portion of your knowledge and information and -- or, rather, dealt with your observations in that statement; but I'd like to ask you about the part that you heard from Ms. Loukas, what you heard from her. You say that in that conversation you had with her, you saw that there were sharp differences between Ms. Loukas and Mr. Stewart. Can you tell the Court briefly what these sharp differences were?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The fundamental sharp difference between them was that Ms. Loukas was bothered by what she perceived as a lack of Defence theory or Defence strategy, a regulating principle that would help the Defence team to set its priorities, determine its short-term and long-term goals, and so on and so forth. She felt frustrated, that was my perception, in the way somebody feels frustrated when they are unable to do what they feel is the right thing under the circumstances or the -- I would add the professionally right thing. She felt professionally frustrated. I think that would be the most succinct way of putting it and the most accurate. That is my perception, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You said that she said that she did not wish to share the blame for the catastrophic results that would ensue. Now, my question to you is this: Do you remember what she said to the Trial Chamber? Do you remember what she said then? Did she say something similar when she handed in her resignation to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the first part of your question, I quote her literally. She used the word "catastrophe." This is not a paraphrase. This is the word Ms. Loukas used in her conversation with me. As for the second part of your question, I probably was there, but I do not recall what you're referring to. I simply don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I say to you that in a certain number of documents and notes made by Mr. Stewart from the meetings with representatives of the Trial Chamber that Mr. Stewart himself made -- said the following: "If I don't get the necessary resources faced with a situation of this kind, I can expect catastrophic results." So did you feel a measure of concern on Mr. Stewart's part as well?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: At the risk of -- I hesitate to say at the risk of disappointing you, but I just have to be absolutely frank and tell the Chamber what I know or what I reliably perceived; and I cannot read Mr. Stewart's mind, I don't know inside how worried or not worried he may have been, but I cannot really say that in any conversation with me that he expressed a sense of foreboding about the possible result of the trial. I cannot recall that at all. He had -- and again I hate to talk this way with respect I have for Mr. Nicholls. It's a different culture, different mentality, and I think we all understand that. But the English do have a certain attitude that they can put on, a care-free attitude. Oh, well, we'll -- you know, we'll manage, that sort of thing. How they actually feel inside, who knows. I'm not English, so it's hard for me to say. So Mr. Stewart may very well have felt concern about the possible outcome of the trial, but he did not really ever express it to me in quite those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: So your answer is that he did not show concern.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, did Mr. Stewart, when you talked to him, intimate what type of -- what area of the law he dealt with in England as Defence counsel? Was it criminal law, commercial law? What area of the law did he deal with as counsel in England?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: What he was mostly dealing with in England, from conversation with him, comments that he made, actually also on the internet you can find out, he did, I think, a lot of commercial law, sports law, thing like that. And also, I find this admirable, I believe that he was involved in international organisations promoting human rights in -- in the Middle East. I believe it was Kurdistan or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now answer hypothetically? Was not Mr. Stewart perhaps concerned about the outcome -- was he not concerned about the outcome because he didn't understand the case fully? Might that have been the case?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, your alternative question, whether he understood it, I think I dealt with that issue in my statement, and it is not really subject to my speculation. I heard him say, and so did Mr. Josse, in the Detention Unit that he did not feel that he understood the case and that he was at a loss to figure out what to do about it, how to conduct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: If I say to you now that in Mr. Stewart's notes we can read that there is a statement by a representative of the Trial Chamber that -- that he -- that he was criticised for putting the burden on Ms. Loukas whereas he was engaged in some private problems and dealt with cases in London, would that be your experience as well and your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not familiar with the document you're referring to, but certainty the issue is familiar to me. From my own observation, while Ms. Loukas was here it did seem to me that whatever may have been the allocation of duties between them that she ended up with more than her fair share, with the proviso that I don't know when they made their deal at the beginning of the trial whether it was 50/50, 60/40, 70/30, or whatever. I have no idea what private arrangement they had, but it certainly seem to me that she was being overworked; and she expressed to me very grave concerns and frustration about that. She felt abused, to be quite frank about it. So definitely that is true. As far as his other professional activities are concern, I do know that on a couple of occasions, not just while Ms. Loukas was here but throughout the period of my tenure, he did spend a few days in London to, as he put it, wrap up some pending cases that he was involved in. I don't know whether that practice went back to the period before I joined the team, but on a couple of occasions he did that while I was here; correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Another question: You told us that Mr. Stewart was not au courant in the case, but did he try to learn about the case, to familiarise himself, or was he in fact in favour of makeshift solutions, and was he not really interested in the case at all?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may take a minute or two to give a bit more elaborate answer to your question. I learned something later on from Mr. Josse that I think is relevant to -- to this question, and it has to do with the way things operate in -- in Great Britain. They have a system which we don't have in America, barristers and solicitors. The solicitor and his staff do most of the preparatory work, serve it on a silver platter to the barrister. The barrister goes to court and presents the results to -- to the Judge. I -- I think that Mr. Stewart was very much a product of that system. He saw himself as a barrister, and he, in the light of the explanation that I later obtain from Mr. Josse of how the British system worked, which was something that I was really not familiar with, not in that detail, I always wondered what a solicitor was and how it differed from being a barrister, then retrospectively I can use that explanatory model to make a lot of his conduct more clear. It is as if he expected the members of his team, including co-counsel, to in effect act as a solicitor, co-counsel as solicitor in some sense and the other members of his team as his assistants, preparing everything, he picks it up, takes it to court and does his part. To return directly to your question, I never had the impression that he tried to do any serious academic work, to learn about the background of the Yugoslav crisis or about the nature of the conflict there. That may be an erroneous impression, but that is the impression that I have. In his home, for example, I -- I just saw two or three books, journalistic work, basically, nothing serious. And in conversation with him, I never had the sense that he had an in-depth knowledge about the background and the underlying issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Now I have a question regarding the documents. When I received the decision from the Appeals Chamber, I received a huge archive. It was delivered to me in the Detention Unit. Now I would like to know about this archive. I don't know. Do you know maybe what the sources of all those documents? Let me be quite specific. Do you know that Mr. Brashich was appointed as my counsel before Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the witness is kindly asked to wait for the interpretation to complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Now I would like to --

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... files from the trial period. Yes, I am familiar indirectly by hearsay so to speak with this issue. Apparently when Mr. Stewart took over the case, he asked Mr. Brashich to send him his work product, and he ended up receiving a couple of boxes of files, discovery material and other case-related files, and many of those boxes were unopened, and obvious conclusion could be drawn from that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Now a specific question. Did your Defence team ever study those documents? Did Mr. Stewart, himself, study it?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to remind you that I arrived in April of 2005, and a lot went on before my joining the team. So I cannot speak about what happen before, but while I was there, the only contact I had with the material in our office at the Dutch Bar Association building was a task that Mr. Stewart gave me over the Christmas holidays in 2005 to spend some time there, a couple of days, sift through a lot of paperwork that was basically strewn all over, lying on the floor, see what I thought was important and preserve it, and I'm trying to think the word he used, but basically it means throw out the rest. So that is the only contact I had with possibly some of that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Did any members of the Defence team ever tell you that the documents had been studied, the documents that they had received from Mr. Brashich and from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, nobody told me that. Which doesn't mean that it wasn't but nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked for the interpretation to end before providing his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You stated here, and this is something that other persons said in their statements, that many of the boxes full of documents were in actual fact out in the -- were actually un-opened, that nobody went through them at all?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: What I can testify about is what I heard from Mr. Stewart for one, that Mr. Brashich sent a number of boxes with documents and that many of those boxes came from Mr. Brashich, from America, unopened, in the same condition presumably that they were when they were sent to Mr. Brashich. That much I know. I cannot really talk about anything else in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Josse, the other co-counsel, and you mentioned that Mr. Stewart sent him to Bosnia and that this was the first time that he actually went there to that area. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether you received from Mr. Josse any information as to what he was able to do, anything useful that he was able to do given his meager knowledge of Bosnian at the time when he went there?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can hardly expect someone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Karganovic, may I interrupt you a moment. I understand that you listen in the language of Mr. Krajisnik, so it's easy for you to answer easily so you should wait a while to let the interpretation to finish before you answer otherwise the interpreters cannot pick up the answer correctly. So please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Where were we? Ah ha, whether Mr. Josse accomplished anything useful in Bosnia. Well, you can hardly expect somebody in Mr. Josse's position to say, "I went there. I didn't accomplish anything." He didn't say that in so many words, but prior to his going there, in the period before the decision was even made to seen him there, in conversation with Mr. Josse he made it clear that while he -- he and his wife enjoyed travelling, they had never been very much anywhere outside of England except maybe to France, that he had never been to the Balkans, and that frankly he knew nothing or next to nothing about the local affairs there. So he was a tabular rasa by his own admission when he went there and the Chamber can figure out for themselves when he joined the case and when he first went to Bosnia, I don't know, two or three months later, how much can you master of this huge material in the meantime. So he went there. May I give my own thoughts here, speculate a little bit, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Depending on what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not going so say anything terrible, just something that I think makes common sense. For instance, Mr. Stewart had a B/C/S speaker on the team, Mr. Jolovic at the time, who was fluent in both English and B/C/S; and I believe he was born in Belgrade, was studying in London, in England, and had extensive familiarity with local issues. So it struck me as very odd when he decided to send Josse to Bosnian. He asked me if I knew anybody who could -- who spoke English who could act as Josse's interpreter there. Well, eventually I found a friend and that worked out, but I thought that it was very odd that he wouldn't send a team member who already had presumably some familiarity with the issues. The friend that I recommended in Bosnia was fine, but he was studying something completely unrelated to anything that we were doing, and he just happen to speak both languages, and to that extent he was useful. So it struck me as a very odd choice on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karganovic, you mentioned and you told the Trial Chamber that there were 20 witnesses who were called. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, if you recall, how many statements had been taken from the witnesses, from potential witnesses? Could you give us a ball-park figure?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes. There were at least 200, and I still have them all in my computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And now let me ask you this: How did the Defence teamwork out the plan to call the 20 witnesses? I apologise, but they tell me that this figure that you just gave us, 200 witnesses, was not recorded in the transcript. Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My answer was that there were about 200 witness statements that were obtained by investigators in the field in Bosnia, Mr. Krajisnik's investigators, that we had to work with, and I have them all in my computer. How -- how did --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: How did you call the witnesses? Could you please explain that to the Trial Chamber? How did you decide to call those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Initially it was a subject of intense negotiation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Stewart, and frequent disagreements. It was hit and miss. Obviously some of the people on -- on -- in -- under the best of circumstances, they were sick or had some family issues, some would not have been able to come anyway, or they would be able to come but later. So you always encounter these bumps in the road. But when you used the word "plan," there really was no plan that I was aware of. It was haphazard. And an illustration of how haphazard this process was is the following: Around January of 2006, the Defence team became pretty desperate because we didn't know how -- on what basis to call witnesses, and so Nicholas said to the person who was in charge of witnesses, "Just take the list and go down the list alphabetically and see whom you could catch."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karganovic, could you please tell to the Trial Chamber whether Krajisnik gave his proposal to Mr. Stewart as to the witnesses that should be called and that you made summaries of?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And were those witnesses called without Krajisnik's knowledge so to speak I was advised only at a later stage how the witnesses were called.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: There were often surprises in it for Mr. Krajisnik. Everything was haphazard. Sometimes he would consult with Mr. Krajisnik, consult in the sense of tell him who would be called, and times somebody would be called and would pop up here. Mr. Krajisnik would be surprise. Or Mr. Krajisnik would be under the impression that another person would be called, and somebody that Mr. Stewart thought was more appropriate was in fact called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karganovic, let me remind you now. Did Krajisnik ask Mr. Stewart to provide him with a list of witnesses that he intends to call?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Please respond. And did he get it?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No. What I mean is did Krajisnik receive from Mr. Stewart a list of witnesses that Mr. Stewart intended to call?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really not sure. We were making and changing witness lists, and again I have all that in my computer. The witness list was in a constant state of flux, so it is very difficult for me to give a precise answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let me ask you now did Krajisnik ask Mr. Stewart to explain to him what was necessary -- what we needed to prepare in order to challenge the indictment?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Was it done more than once?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: How did Mr. Stewart respond to that? Did he provide an answer?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my previous answer is not complete. I think it's very important. I said, "Quite a few times." I was never present when Mr. Stewart may have provided a complete answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I hope that we agree that you were the only person interpreting the conversations between me and Mr. Stewart. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I do, conditionally. Don't forget that other B/C/S speakers joined our team later on, including Mr. Sladojevic and another person. So later on into 2006 we would sometimes take turn going -- turns going to the Detention Unit. So I can only speak about what went on in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: So your response is that in your presence while you were there Mr. Stewart did not give Krajisnik an answer to this demand of Krajisnik as to what needed to be done to challenge the indictment and to mount a defence?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what was the difference in the views held by Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: One fundamental difference in their approaches was that Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps in a business-like fashion, kept insisting on creating a defence plan, conducting a thorough analysis of the -- of the Prosecution case in relation to the indictment and then devising effective counter-measures, so to speak, which we would implement through our case, the Defence case. And as I point out in my statement, which would be in one of the paragraphs where I say that after the July break in 2006 we had about two months before the resumption of the trial, and during that period, until September, I believe in September I took about ten days and -- off and went to Turkey with my cousin, but between then and sometime in September, Mr. -- Mr. Stewart and I visited Mr. Krajisnik quite often at the Detention Unit, and there were two major -- well, three major topics that were discussed. One that was put on the table by Mr. Krajisnik was devising a defence plan. Two, that where promoted by Mr. Stewart budget, the financial issues, and not allowing the practice of Mr. Krajisnik asking witnesses questions to be continued into the Defence case. So it was a dialogue of the deaf with me in between. Neither side really heard the other or paid much attention to what the other was saying. It was two agonising months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Let me ask you this now: You said before the Trial Chamber that you did not made your views public - I'm referring to the things that you put in your statement - simply because you did not want your relationship with Mr. Stewart to be changed, so to speak, to be disturbed in any way. An unusual question: As a professional, did you feel that your loyalty towards Mr. Stewart is something that is binding and prevents you from going public with those things?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know how you want to define loyalty, but I do feel a sense of personal sympathy with Nicholas because he's an exceptionally nice and sympathetic person. And if you mean that my not wanting to cause him hurt or harm had something to do with it, it probably did; but as well, I don't think that I really had enough time to reflect on all these things while it was going on, while the trial was going on, to -- to put everything together and to say, well, the -- in the interests of justice I need to do this or something like that, putting personal feelings and loyalties aside. It was later on that it struck me that perhaps writing a statement on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf listing my observations would be a good idea and -- and the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You attended the trial, the hearings. Did you -- were you at the trial when Krajisnik presented his -- this agreement with Mr. Stewart out in public and addressed the Trial Chamber to that effect?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: When you asked that Nicholas be dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could we say that I disagreed with what Mr. Stewart was doing?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is the only possible conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now since we have very little time left, I would like to ask you this: When you joined Mr. Stewart's team, on whose recommendation, on whose orders -- let me put it this way: It is quite usual here for the lead counsel to appoint his or her associates. Did Mr. Stewart do that while you were here? Did he hire you?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course he hired me. That's the procedure. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I can go on. I think your question was how did he get a hold of me. Well, he knew me from before. We had run into each other around the time when he took over the case. As a freelance interpreter for the Tribunal, I went with him to see Mr. Krajisnik at the Detention Unit on a couple of occasions while the issue of whether or not he would take up the case was being debated. So he knew me. And apparently there was a falling out with my predecessor, and he called me and asked me. He said, "I'm looking into possible candidates, so I'm talking to one right now but I'm not so sure whether he would be able to do it. Would you be available?" And that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In your statement you say that you're not in any kind of conflict and that Mr. Stewart indeed is not angry with you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I hope he is not angry at me. In fact, I see no reason why he should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'm just repeating what you said in your statement. Now let me ask you this, but I'd like to make a short introduction first, and it is linked to the statement that you gave to the Judges with respect to expert witnesses. What you said is this: You said that on several occasions I insisted on calling a larger number of expert witnesses because I considered that if we looked at it logically, if the Prosecution called not five or six but nine expert witnesses, then I thought that we should bring in nine too, and then I reduced the number. Now, there's a story that we like to recount in my part of the world and it is this: Somebody who didn't know what something good is knows what it's expensive. Now, what would be your answer? If Stewart saw that the Prosecution has distinguished lawyers and that if they saw fit to call nine expert witnesses, what prompted him not to call a single expert witness, especially as we have papers here saying that Judge Orie was wondering why expert witnesses were not called? So what do you think prompted Mr. Stewart to decide not to call expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I would prefer to keep to the level of reporting as empirically as possible, and I have already said what Mr. Stewart's explanation was in so many words, said to me for his decision not to call expert witnesses. I think that is the best answer that I can give, because if I went beyond that it would be my personal speculation and that would not be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Can you repeat his answer, please -- or, rather, repeat your answer. Why would he would not call expert witnesses if the example had been set by the Prosecution in calling expert witnesses? Was he just not interested in doing that? Was he disinterested? Did he consider this to be part of his strategy or who knows what else? So could you look at those alternatives and tell us what you think?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly did not have the impression that the decision not to call expert witnesses was the result of a sophisticated strategic decision. The way he motivated it was simply by saying that in his view they would not have anything substantial to contribute to the Defence case, and Mr. Josse was present on several occasion when these views were stated by -- by Nicholas, and that's as far as I can go really. That's the only -- the only statement that he ever made that comes to the level of an explanation for all its worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And I think I concluded one minute ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. I will now -- Judge Shahabuddeen, you have a question now. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Karganovic, if you are in charge of the case would you have called all 200 of the witnesses whom you mentioned, or would you have pruned the list a little?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that I feel exceptionally honoured that even hypothetically you put me in the position of being in charge of the case. Thank you very much. I am -- I would not be up to it, but it's nice to think about something like that. But specifically in response to your question, I definitely would not have called all 200 witnesses, and I definitely would have pruned the list. I don't think that to do a good job you -- you have to call one witness for each Prosecution witness. Quality is much more important than quantity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, a follow-up question is this: I was struck by your statement to the effect that Mr. Stewart simply said, "Follow the list in alphabetical order and there you have it." Now, later on you said that the list was constantly in a state of making and changing. It was also constantly in a state of flux. Does that mean that he did not apply to the decision of the order in which witnesses should be called, a simple mechanical rule of thumb in terms of statement of you should call them in alphabetical order but that he applied some other criterion? What is your observation on that?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I did not have the impression that he had a criterion. In fact, I took his instruction to go alphabetically as a cry of desperation which indicated in pretty clear terms that there was no criterion and that he perhaps was at a loss how to devise one. That was my reaction to that instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, first of all may I say that I opened up by asking you to consider the matter on the basis that if you were in charge of the case. So I recognise very fully that you were not, in fact, in charge of the case. Now, may I ask your attention to this: You referred to Ms. Loukas, and you recalled her statement to the effect that something would be a catastrophe. May I just clarify my own thoughts to the effect that you were not saying that she said that to Mr. Stewart or to the Trial Chamber, but she said that to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She very definitely said that to me. She said, to expand a little bit on her statement, that she felt that the outcome of the trial would be a catastrophe and that professionally she did not want to be associate with it and that this was one of the major reasons for her decision to leave the team. As far as the other dimension of your question, I think it refers back to something that Mr. Krajisnik asked. I'm sure I was there when she made her statement, announced her intention to -- to leave the team. I don't know what terminology she used, but personally I do not remember her using the word "catastrophe," but it's very simple. One can check the record. But if she didn't use the word "catastrophe," I'm sure she used something dramatic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: She didn't use that word to Mr. Stewart or to the Trial Chamber. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, assuming -- and I believe that I was there when she addressed the Chamber on that issue. I do not recall her using that word. As far as her interaction with Mr. Stewart is concerned, she did not use that particular word in my presence. Privately, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now turn to Mr. Dershowitz for questioning briefly the witness on JCE-related matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Karganovic, I'd like to start with the end then work a little bit backwards. Assuming again that you were elevated to the position of running the operation, do you believe that the witnesses who were actually called were the most qualified, and you believe that they were chosen because of strategic decisions that they would be the most helpful to accomplish the goals and objectives of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: My answer to your question is no. Many of the witnesses we called may have been qualified to talk about micro-issues and something that may have happened in some municipality that nobody had ever heard of, but as far as the larger and determinative issues in the case, they had very little, if anything, to say about them or to have an impact on them by means of their testimony. I can tell you that at some point we discussed, I mean the Defence team, we discussed the notion of maybe inviting a few high-profile witnesses who were involved in the political negotiating process before and during the conflict to show that Mr. Krajisnik was oriented towards finding peaceful solutions to -- to these issues that were tearing Bosnia apart, and the names that were mentioned think I were quite logical. Cutileiro was very important. Stoltenberg, also very important. And Mitsotakis, the former Prime Minister of Greece. And it just so happens that my cousin is married to a Greek, lives on the island of Crete in the town of Kanji [phoen] and is a neighbour and friend of Mr. Mitsotakis. So while all this was being talked about, I contacted my cousin and she say, "Sure. I will talk to him, and I'm sure he'll be happy to accept an invitation to testify." So at least we could have had him. I'm confident also that Cutileiro and Stoltenberg probably would have responded favourably. However, as happened on quite a few occasions when ideas were floated, they were discussed for a while and then simply dropped, and this was dropped as well. So we had people from nondescript municipalities, but we didn't have Cutileiro.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Are you then saying there were no strategic judgements that you're aware of not to call those witnesses that you've just listed, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: With respect to experts, and I assume there you would have done some pruning of the experts, do you know if the decision not to call experts was made for solely strategic reasons?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot think of any sensible strategic reason, but then I'm committed not to reading other people's minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Well, do you know whether these expert witnesses were interviewed and whether the substance of what they would testify to is available before the decision was made not to call them?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any prospective expert witness being contacted, much less interviewed, other than Mrs. Radovanovic. So the decision not to call these other hypothetical expert witnesses was made sight unseen, not because it was felt that they were unqualified or that they would not be able to do a good report or anything like that. An attempt was never made to locate them, let alone interview them.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: You have testified with respect to the fact that you didn't know of a strategy or a goal. I'd like to focus specifically on the question of JCE.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stewart, in your presence, ever address the question as to what the Prosecutors would have to prove in order to establish a JCE and what defences could be available to prevent them from carrying their burden of proof with respect to JCE?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The closest that I heard Nicholas come to a serious discussion of how we might save Mr. Krajisnik from destruction was when he commented on one occasion, it was in the Detention Unit, that what we should do is to try to put as much distance between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic. In other words, that they were as separate in their activities, their lines of work, and in their personal lives as possible, and that this would be an important element in relieving Mr. Krajisnik of excessive liability or guilt that might come his way as a result of his perceived association with Dr. Karadzic. That's the only discussion of that nature that I've heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Was that discussion specifically keyed into JCE, or was it a more generalised conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was part of a generalised conversation. In fact, I heard Nicholas refer to JCE very few times. I -- it was not a topic that was in the forefront of attention. In fact -- well, it's like in a war. You don't know where the enemy will attack, but in fact the Defence was more wary of the expanded Presidency issue as a mechanism of liability than JCE. So I think we spent more time talking about whether or not there was an expanded Presidency and whether Mr. Krajisnik had anything to do with it than JCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: You testified that Mr. Krajisnik was asking for detailed information about a defence. Did he ever raise the question in your presence while you were acting as a translator as to what the elements or ingredients or aspects were of JCE and ask for an explanation from counsel as what that was?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And did he ever get an answer to that question in your presence?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I do not recall his ever getting a coherent answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And did he ask that question more than once?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Are you aware of any assignments that were given during the year and one-month period that you were the case manager to anyone on the Defence team to specifically address JCE as a legal concept and/or to then do a factual analysis of JCE in terms of the defence?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: It did not come to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Now again you had meetings both with Mr. Stewart but also at least once a week there were meetings to discuss steps that had to be taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And at no time during your meetings with Mr. Stewart or during the weekly meetings did the question of JCE ever come up or the legal work discussed or the factual work that had to be done in order to address JCE; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Especially the latter part of your question. I mean the concept may have been fleetingly mentioned, but I think really your question is was any serious consideration given to it both theoretically and practically. Not to my knowledge. Not in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And just the final question and that is did Mr. Stewart ever try to secure from you any information about your knowledge of the period from 1990 to 1992, and were you ever asked to pull together materials that would be a Defence statement of fact or a Defence view or Defence approach with respect to that period?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: And do you know of anyone else who was asked to do that during the year and one month that you were case manager?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand there are no questions from the Bench, so I will turn to the Prosecutor, Mr. Kremer, for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Mr. Karganovic, is it fair to say that in response to the Prosecution case the Defence approach was prove everything?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There were no admissions made and the Prosecution was put to the challenge of proving every fact that it alleged in the indictment against Mr. Krajisnik? Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I understand your question now, and it may go back to -- to the issue of agreed upon facts where I was not involved. So I came into the case, I think, too late to be able to give a competent answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Just accept my statement that there were no agreed facts, and in the absence of agreed facts is it fair to say that the Defence, at least when you saw it, was, "Prove everything, Prosecution"?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: That is a possible conclusion and probably a fair one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. And in terms of the defence, you raised the question of expanded Presidency. That was certainly an issue that was under active discussion during the course of not only the Prosecution case but also in preparation for the Defence case, yes?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And also you mentioned the distance between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. I assume that the Defence saw Mr. Karadzic's role in this much more serious than they saw Mr. Krajisnik's role; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it would be fairer to say that the Defence, not having had such a clear picture of Mr. Krajisnik's role, who knows -- and by "Defence," I basically mean Mr. Stewart, who knows what picture they had of the role of Dr. Karadzic? I think that his thought was that as long as Mr. Krajisnik was portrayed in his official capacity as president of parliament, without any executive responsibility, he would be in a better position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Correct. And during the Prosecution case and during the Defence case that is, in fact, how they attempted to portray Mr. Krajisnik. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: That is just president of parliament without any other responsibilities of any importance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Right. And that is Mr. Krajisnik's essential defence on appeal. That's his ground of appeal. "The Trial Chamber got it wrong. I had no authority." Is that is not right?

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if I have standing to object, but I don't think Mr. Kremer is the one to described what the main point on the appeal is, nor do I think Mr. Krajisnik -- I mean Mr. Karganovic is. I think that's really for the Chamber to make a determination on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may chime in, I believe that I'm here to testify along the lines of my statement about my observations during the trial. Of course I'm familiar with Mr. Krajisnik's appeal, but I would not feel that it is my role here to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did you or did you not assist Mr. Krajisnik in filing his appeal?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And in fact, your statement that you're testifying to today suggests that it is an addendum to Mr. Krajisnik's appeal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that the statement that you prepared was prepared after discussions with Mr. Krajisnik and all of the specific grounds that he had put in his notice of appeal with your assistance.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, not at all. I wrote my statement myself without any reference to his appeal or his grounds of appeal. It is based on my observations while I was case manager during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: But you put it in these terms: "I will describe in my experience and impressions gained while I was a member of his Defence team during trial proceedings which refer to the specific claims that Mr. Krajisnik made in his appeal."

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that your statement is designed and written particularly to blend in to the specific claims that Mr. Krajisnik has made in his notice of appeal prepared with your assistance. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with that. There may be points of compatibility between my statement and Mr. Krajisnik's appeal, but my statement was not generated as adjunct to his appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: When you prepare the statement did you had before you or had you read Mr. Mano's statement that was prepared September 23rd, 2004?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall having had his statement. And his statement had no influence whatsoever on my impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You did not take from Mr. Mano's statement the suggestion that Mr. Stewart was fairly uninterested in historical and factual background of the case?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You did not take from Mr. Mano's statement that Stewart was paying visits to European cities and working in his practice in London?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not need the assistance of Mr. Mano or to read his statement to point those things out because it was a matter of simple observation and other members of the Defence team observed exactly same things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Ms. Loukas, you indicated on the Davidovic issue that you communicated to her the results of your conversation with the doctor who was the husband of the other doctor whose equipment allegedly went missing.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: What specifically did you tell Ms. Loukas about your telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I told Ms. Loukas that the doctor said that the extortion that was alleged on the part of Mr. Davidovic did not take place. The doctor denied the allegation that was made by Mr. Krajisnik's investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. And you were present in court when the allegation was put to Davidovic about this fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes. And when Ms. Loukas put the allegation to him knowing it to be false, did you stand up and correct the record?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it is my role to intervene during a trial in -- in such a manner. Ms. Loukas was conducting the examination, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying that you were -- you were privy to some unethical conduct and Ms. Loukas' behalf? Did you report this to Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. N. DERSHOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. It presupposes that Ms. Loukas knew it was false solely because the victim denied it. That may or may not have been the case. It's a question what she knew, and I think it's unfair to ask this witness that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'll ask it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Stewart that you were concerned about the cross-examination that was being actively objected to by the Prosecution, continuing when you had told her that the witness did not stand by the investigator's statement?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence, meaning both Ms. Loukas and Mr. Stewart, were both aware of the outcome of my telephone call, and the speculation was that Mr. Davidovic was such a powerful and intimidating figure that even though these people may have been hurt by him, they did not dare to talk about it. So that was their view of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And you're aware of the fact, because you were in court, that at some point after the 27th of June, 2005, Mr. Stewart withdrew those specific questions on the basis that they had no -- they had no substantiation; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no specific recollection, but I believe if you say so it's a matter of record, but I just want to emphasise that I have nothing to do with it because I was not in charge of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You have never been a practising lawyer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And in your CV when you refer to yourself as having been a public defender, that's inaccurate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: What is accurate is that I worked for the office of the public defender in Oceanside, California for a private firm, which did contract work for the public defender; and I performed the duties that I indicated in my CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: So then your CV is inaccurate in that it refers to the office of the public defender in San Diego County because that is not who you worked for; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not so sure you're correct in that, because all of us in that office, insofar as we dealt with public defenders' work, were paid by the office of the public defender, i.e., the State of California.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: You refer to the San Diego County, and I'm informed by the letter that is AP2 that the department of the public defender in its present form was only established in 1988. So you could not have worked for them in 1991 to 1994. How do you explain that.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no need to explain it because it was very definitely a department of the public defender in California in San Diego County and it contracted the office that I worked for in Oceanside and referred work to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you also in your CV refer to the fact that you're in private practice but you weren't in private practice as a lawyer, were you?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Where is that.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: That was Seattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In Washington?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, you also refer to the fact that you were a legal assistant on the Dragan Obrenovic Defence team. You were not a legal assistant for the Dragan Obrenovic Defence team, were you?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm going to refer you to a letter written by Eugene Wilson. David Eugene Wilson. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And I believe you've seen this letter.

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'll just read something that he says. Did you ever -- before I do that, did you ever represent to him that you'd practised law?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In a letter that Mr. Wilson wrote to Mr. Petrov in the Popovic case, he says: "In his interview with me, Mr. Karganovic told me that he was a licensed attorney having graduated from law school in either Illinois or Indiana," and then he has, "which I cannot remember now, and that he had served as a public defender in California. He stated that he no longer practiced law since he had decided that he did not enjoy being a lawyer but preferred being an interpreter in the Serbian and Spanish languages." And he said, "I made no attempt to verify his status credentials as a law school graduate and a licensed attorney," because he hired you as a translator interpreter at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct he initially hired me as a translator and interpreter then I became case manager and legal assistant in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And so you're saying that Mr. Wilson, who is a partner in a law firm and describes himself as being a senior prosecutor in the State of Washington for the federal government, a magistrate for eight years and is now a senior partner in one of the large law firms in Seattle, he's got to wrong?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Partially. Now, when you left the Obrenovic team, where did you get employment?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: With the Stanisic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And how long did you work for the Stanisic team?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: That was for about a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And why was your employment terminated?

utterances.speaker: STEFAN KARGANOVIC
